In this article
Text Link
Learning and development practitioners have a particular superpower. We take complex topics and make them clear, useful, and worth someone’s attention.
So yes, we’re picky about “insights.” There’s a lot of noise out there. The same ideas, endlessly recycled, and thin takes dressed up as thought leadership.
The challenge isn’t finding content. It’s knowing what’s worth paying attention to — and what actually helps you design learning that works in real organizations.
That’s why we put this list together. Some are blogs. Others are newsletters, Substacks, or insight hubs.
We try to hold our own blog to the same standard.
Happy reading!

✨ The List

One Useful Thing

Dr. Philippa Hardman

Steal These Thoughts!

eLearning Coach

Abstract (Maestro)

MAAS Marketing

Offbeat Works

Ness Labs

People Managing People

eLearning Industry

LinkedIn Talent Blog

Spotify HR: Learning & Growth

How to use this list
Pick one category that matches what you’re working on right now, then choose one or two sources to follow for the next few weeks.
As you read, save the pieces that come with something you can actually use — a framework, an example, a checklist, a prompt.
Each resource includes a “Try this” to help you turn an idea into a small experiment. Keep it contained, run it within a week or two, and write down what changed.
AI and modern learning design
AI is changing how work gets done
, which means it’s changing what “good” learning looks like. These reads help you stay grounded, test assumptions, and build workflows that hold up beyond the hype.
1. One Useful Thing
(Ethan Mollick)

In their words:
“Trying to understand the implications of AI for work, education, and life.”
Why we like it:
it’s consistently clear-eyed. Curious, but never credulous.
Great for:
deciding what actually changes (and what doesn’t) in how people learn and work gets done.
🧪 Try this:
In your next team meeting, share one post 24 hours ahead. Spend 7 minutes: 2 mins “what surprised you,” 3 mins “what changes for us,” 2 mins to pick one rule to adopt (e.g., “AI use must be disclosed in learner-facing materials”). Write it into your team norms doc.
2. Dr. Phil's Newsletter
(Dr. Philippa Hardman)
In their words:
“I talk about the intersection between human and machine learning (aka AI).”
Why we like it:
it brings rigor to modern tools. Frameworks show up early, and they hold.
Great for:
designing AI-supported learning that still meets a high bar for effectiveness.
🧪 Try this:
Pick one framework and convert it into a one-page “definition of done” for a module (objectives, practice, feedback, measurement). Use it on the next asset you ship and do a 15-minute QA against the checklist before publishing.
3. Steal These Thoughts!
(Ross Stevenson)

In their words:
“Get the best insights, tools & templates for the modern L&D pro.”
Why we like it:
it’s direct. It helps you cut through the fog when plans get abstract.
Great for:
simplifying overbuilt learning initiatives and refocusing teams on what will actually change behavior.
🧪 Try this:
Take one issue and run a 10-minute “simplify sprint.” List the current plan in 5 bullets, then cut it to 3. End by deleting or pausing one deliverable you’re doing “because we always do it.”
Learning craft
This is the category for improving the quality of what you ship. Less “more content,” more clarity, retention, and
learner experience that respects attention
.
4. The eLearning Coach
(Connie Malamed)

In their words:
“I’m Connie Malamed, the publisher of The eLearning Coach website and podcast.”
Why we like it:
it makes research usable. The writing is clear, and the advice travels well.
Great for:
improving clarity, retention, and learner understanding.
🧪 Try this:
Choose one lesson and rewrite one screen using Connie’s principle (chunking, signaling, visuals). Then do a 5-person hallway test: ask learners to summarize the key point in one sentence. If fewer than 4/5 get it, revise once.
5. Abstract
(Maestro)

In their words:
“A newsletter designed to inform and inspire learning professionals.”
Why we like it:
it’s a sharp filter. You get signal without losing an afternoon to browsing.
Great for:
scanning what matters across learning, design, and tech without losing time to browsing.
🧪 Try this:
Each week, pick one item and turn it into a single pilot card: “What we’ll try,” “who it’s for,” “success metric,” “date we’ll review.” Keep pilots to 2 weeks max. Review on Fridays.
Adoption and engagement
Good learning doesn’t matter if no one uses it. These reads help you treat learning like a product: position it, market it internally, and
design for uptake
.
6. MAAS Marketing

In their words:
“MAAS Marketing transforms People Functions into strategic growth engines…”
Why we like it:
it treats engagement like a design problem, not a participation problem.
Great for:
increasing adoption of learning programs by treating them like internal products.
🧪 Try this:
For your next program launch, create a
3-message sequence
:
Problem + stakes
(why this matters),
What to do
(one clear action),
Proof
(testimonial/data point).
Send across two channels (Slack + email). Track clicks + completions for one week.
Practitioner lenses
This category is intentionally eclectic. It’s here to stretch your defaults, expose you to different working styles, and give you ideas worth pressure-testing, not blindly copying.
7. Offbeat Works
In their words:
“An L&D newsletter you’ll love. Every Sunday we send over a pack of articles, e-books, podcasts, videos, and thoughts… to inspire you and help you stay up to date with what’s happening within our L&D community.”
Why we like it:
it widens the aperture. You get a steady mix of voices and angles, which is exactly what keeps your thinking from getting stale.
Great for:
discovery when you’re early in a problem, or when you want fresh inputs before committing to a direction.
‍
🧪 Try this:
Pick one idea from Sunday’s pack and run a “smallest test.” Example: add one reflection prompt to a session, or change one onboarding touchpoint. Write a 3-bullet recap: what we changed, what we observed, what we’ll keep.
8. Ness Labs
In their words:
“Ness Labs is a playground for curiosity.”
Why we like it:
it nudges you toward experiments instead of proclamations. Thoughtful, but still practical.
Great for:
building lightweight team habits that improve learning and reflection.
🧪 Try this:
Start a 2-week “learning log” ritual: every Friday, team members post 3 lines in a shared channel — “what I tried,” “what I learned,” “what I’ll do next.” At the end, turn the best 5 lines into a “team playbook” note.
Industry pulse
Use these to scan what’s being talked about broadly, then go deeper with the more opinionated sources above. They’re great for discovery and mapping the landscape, not for taking every idea at face value.
9. People Managing People

In their words:
“Equips forward-thinking leaders with AI-era strategies, systems, and tools…”
Why we like it:
it’s broad in a useful way. It helps you see what keeps resurfacing across HR and people leadership.
Great for:
spotting recurring patterns in people and talent strategy.
🧪 Try this:
Use it as discovery, then force a filter. Save three articles, pick one to apply, and write a short “context check”:
what’s different about our org that might break this?
Only then design a single pilot.
10. eLearning Industry

In their words:
“The largest online community of eLearning professionals in the industry.”
Why we like it:
it’s a fast landscape view. Helpful when you need quick orientation.
Great for:
quickly mapping the landscape, then narrowing options before making tool or approach decisions.
🧪 Try this:
When you’re researching tools or approaches, create a comparison grid with 4 columns: “use case,” “risk,” “what good looks like,” “questions for vendors.” Fill it using two articles, then validate with one operator source before deciding.
Learning at scale
This is where you go when you need to design for real organizational constraints: complexity, consistency, stakeholder alignment, and programs that survive contact with the business.
11. LinkedIn Talent Blog

In their words:
“Your source for remarkable recruiting strategies, tips and trends.”
Why we like it:
it speaks stakeholder. It connects skills and talent priorities to language leaders already use.
Great for:
translating skills and talent trends into language and priorities stakeholders already understand.
🧪 Try this:
Bring one post to a stakeholder meeting as a conversation starter: “If this trend is real, what capability do we need most?” Capture answers on one slide and turn them into a top-3 priority list for next quarter.
12. Spotify HR Blog: Learning & Growth

In their words:
“In this blog, we showcase how we do just that at Spotify.”
Why we like it:
it’s concrete. Real programs, real constraints, and lessons that feel earned.
Great for:
designing programs that hold up inside complex organizations with real constraints.
🧪 Try this:
Pick one story and rewrite it as a two-paragraph internal memo: “What problem we’re solving” + “How we’ll know it worked.” Share it with one partner team and ask one question: “What would stop this from working here?”
A note from us
The voices behind Synthesia’s blog are L&D practitioners with a mix of backgrounds.
We spend a lot of time around AI and tools, but the goal is always the same: better learning that works in complex organizations.
Most of what we publish comes from the same problems you’re likely dealing with — making communication clearer, helping people get up to speed faster, and designing learning that actually holds up once it meets the real world.
If you’re reading along, we’d love to connect on LinkedIn. And if there’s something we should be reading, send it our way.
Amy Vidor
Amy Vidor, PhD is a Learning & Development Evangelist at Synthesia, where she researches learning trends and helps organizations apply AI at scale. With 15 years of experience, she has advised companies, governments, and universities on skills.

8 Best How-To Video Examples
Written by
Kevin Alster
November 7, 2023
Create AI videos with 240+ avatars in 160+ languages.
Get started for FREE
In this article
Text Link
How-to videos are among the most popular in online search results. And they're continuously gaining even more eyes.
On YouTube, the social media network with the
second-highest traffic
in the world, videos directed towards "beginners" that teach how to do new things had a
50%
increase in average daily views since 2020.
But what separates an average how-to video from a great one? And what can you do to ensure your
instructional videos
are nothing short of legendary?
Below is a selection of the best how-to video examples and
templates
to get your creative gears turning 😉.
Who can benefit from a how-to video?
Anyone from independent content creators to companies selling physical/digital products benefits from creating this type of content that nearly
30% of internet users
want to see.
A how-to video could be anything from a marketing video to a video tutorial. Some companies even use them to create explainer videos, a great tool for advertising!
How-to videos are helpful for both external and internal uses. With them, you can:
✅ Teach others about products, services, or concepts
✅ Introduce employees to internal processes
✅ Guide customers through troubleshooting steps
✅ Make tedious procedures easier to learn
✅ And much more!

The 4 different styles of how-to videos

Learn the four styles of how-to videos you can create for your business. Then, use them by default or mix and match as you like.

1. How to troubleshoot your internet connection
5.16 billion people
use the internet, but only a few can tackle a faulty internet connection.
This how-to video
succinctly guides you through the process of troubleshooting without confusing tech jargon.
{lite-youtube videoid="cH4Y5iwDi2M" style="background-image: url(' https://img.youtube.com/vi/cH4Y5iwDi2M/hqdefault.jpg '); " }
Did you notice?
Supplementary video footage demonstrates the narration in slow motion. The visuals make it much easier to follow along with the real-world steps.
Why this example works for how-to videos:
The
video script
follows a simple structure with 3 points, subsequent steps for each point, a recap, and a final recommendation.
The black-and-white
background
contrast and the absence of sound effects make it easy to focus on the information.
The visuals clearly illustrate the instructions spoken by the presenter.
2. How to use Slack
This video recording product tour
is a great example of how you can teach viewers a new software. Packed full of actionable tips, it's useful for onboarding new customers and employees alike.
{lite-youtube videoid="tyg_mLJFo9o" style="background-image: url(' https://img.youtube.com/vi/tyg_mLJFo9o/hqdefault.jpg '); " }
Did you notice?
This is one of those video tutorials that's rich with information thanks to it's easy-to-follow screencast. When looking to make your own effective tutorial video, it's worth
learning how to use a screen recording tool.
Why this example of instructional video is so compelling:
It's a screen recording demonstration, making information transfer more efficient.
The features show in a logical sequence, starting from the specific action of chatting with the team within a channel.
There's a perfect sync between visuals and the narrator's tips without any fluff.
3. How to manage your anger
This is one of those YouTube video examples that raises awareness for a broad audience. It shows how anger impacts physical health and provides relevant content and tips on prevention and management.
{lite-youtube videoid="BsVq5R_F6RA" style="background-image: url(' https://img.youtube.com/vi/BsVq5R_F6RA/hqdefault.jpg '); " }
Did you notice?
The video presents a step-by-step process as a visual journey using emotive storytelling. In one video, you're going from being angry to understanding what this does to you and maintaining your calmness. Meanwhile, you're assured it's okay, you're not alone, this isn't helping you, and you can change.
Why this is one of the most impactful explainer video examples:
The message-tone congruence is excellent, with the whole narration flowing in a laid-back tone.
The detailed action plan is supported with text-on-screen and animated visuals.
The
video content
facilitates information retention with a brief recap and a specific CTA.
4. How to apologize for a mistake
This talking-head YouTube video will strike a chord in many. And it's one of those video examples that also know how to catch your eye.
{lite-youtube videoid="BIlbp2YK86o" style="background-image: url(' https://img.youtube.com/vi/BIlbp2YK86o/hqdefault.jpg '); " }
Did you notice?
This is one of those instructional videos that has a charismatic presenter with an expressive mime. It uses fast-paced sound effects that almost prevent you from noticing it's an 8-minute talk. And it relies on solid structural elements. These elements perfectly combine when you're creating videos for the YouTube platform.
Why this video facilitates information retention:
The objection is covered early, so the viewers can focus on the tips provided instead of dwelling on
Why shouldn't I say 'Sorry
'?
It shows attention to detail, featuring a clean background, uplifting sound effects, and clear narration through a lavalier microphone.
Typography is minimal, focused on the essentials, with the presenter filling all the space between the key moments of words popping on the screen.
5. How to achieve financial well-being
This is one of those
video examples
that prove you can do a lot in a few minutes. Though short, it makes the viewers interested in attaining financial well-being feel more confident.
From
video design
to actual content, it strikes through simplicity, just like great explainer videos should do. And by the end of it, you get the feeling that you know what to do.
{lite-youtube videoid="16lgKUSqrPM" style="background-image: url(' https://img.youtube.com/vi/16lgKUSqrPM/hqdefault.jpg '); " }
Did you notice?
In only six slides, the video tells you everything. At first, you discover what you'll learn. To better illustrate the utility of its topic, the video also introduces a thinking exercise that's designed to improve conversion rates among potential customers.
Then, you learn the three concepts that serve as how-to steps in the video. Finally, you're sent away with actionable steps to achieve each of them.
Why this video offers a clear and compelling message:
It's simple and on point, leaving no room for confusion.
It flows well, with logical steps and a final recap of the key knowledge.
The video content subtly conveys the idea of financial savviness and well-being.
6. "How-to" medical demonstration
From the many video examples out there, animations are among the most attractive. Especially when they reveal complex information you can't see with the naked eye, their effect is remarkable.
With its magnetic visuals, this great explainer video will have you staring in awe. You don't even need to know this demonstrates how the "MegaVac mechanical thrombectomy system" captures and removes blood clots to watch it hypnotized.
{lite-youtube videoid="gWAXOD29YDU" style="background-image: url(' https://img.youtube.com/vi/gWAXOD29YDU/hqdefault.jpg '); " }
Did you notice?
This video is a great way to demonstrate how a product or service works.
If you're in a technical field, this template is perfect for replicating, especially when tackling educational content with overly complex ideas. Great tutorial videos help the audience visualize the process, and animations greatly help.
In this case, the topic is a medical intervention. To explain it to a patient, it would require some medical jargon. And even when described in plain terms, it's hard to picture it. But not when you demonstrate it with a how-to video like this one.
Why this example is perfect for explaining complex concepts:
It starts with powerful imagery that will hook the viewers.
Information flows easily, and the on-screen text matches the visuals.
It pairs animation with explanations from a medical thought leader for increased credibility.
7. How to prepare for an offsite company retreat
This instructional video
is an excellent example of business communication with a hint of pleasure.
While a company offsite retreat announcement, you can convert it into any other type of video announcement in a how-to format.
Think of "How to use our new app," "How to use this new feature on our website," "How to check if you qualify for the new bonuses," or other topics that will fit your internal marketing strategy or brand awareness campaigns.
{lite-youtube videoid="1-Cj7c1dUCA" style="background-image: url(' https://img.youtube.com/vi/1-Cj7c1dUCA/hqdefault.jpg '); " }
Did you notice?
The presentation begins with excitement, moves to the preparation steps, and handles potential concerns. This natural flow helps viewers to focus on the message without obsessing over their unsolved problems. Ultimately, the video script returns to peaking excitement, facilitating information retention and making the instructional video more memorable.
Why this explainer video template is perfect for company announcements:
It's an instructional video with clear steps for the planning stage, accompanied by a "For further questions" resource.
The rich visuals ramp up the excitement and show the travel itinerary in four steps.
It informs and entices in a business-casual tone, subtly strengthening the company's brand.
8. How to scam people for money ;)
We have to admit this how-to video won't wow you with its visuals, but the concept will make you curious. After all, it has scored 431K YouTube views so far.
Were all those YouTube searches aimed at actual "How to scam people for money" educational content? Probably not, and this video certainly isn't about that.
{lite-youtube videoid="e-lWvcEECTY" style="background-image: url(' https://img.youtube.com/vi/e-lWvcEECTY/hqdefault.jpg '); " }
Did you notice?
This YouTube video uses a unique approach to raising awareness on a hot topic. The way it was planned shows a great understanding of what gets the viewers excited.
Specifically, the video speaks to people who follow this YouTube channel for marketing tips. The target audience appreciates an out-of-the-box messaging approach. The video's comments section shows the viewers understand what the creator did with this video.
Why this video gets significant engagement from the audience:
It relies on reverse psychology and gets the viewers intrigued right from the title.
The mean/devilish video theme goes along nicely with the topic.
The step-by-step structure and the surprising visuals that pair with the narration in each slide hook the audience.

How-to video template 🖼

Many of the how-to video examples you see online can be easily recreated with this template. Want to present a product or service? Or to outline a process step-by-step?
Consider this example template
.

{lite-youtube videoid="7qAUWRvvzSA" style="background-image: url(' https://img.youtube.com/vi/7qAUWRvvzSA/hqdefault.jpg '); " }
Start working on your how-to video
Effective how-to videos focus on a clear topic and show you how to achieve something in a logical sequence of steps.
Use this basic framework and spice it up with creative elements to create videos that educate and entertain your audience, all with Synthesia AI. Click here to try out the
free AI video maker
for yourself.

Kevin Alster is a Strategic Advisor at Synthesia, helping enterprises apply generative AI to learning, communication, and performance. With over a decade in education and media, he’s built programs for General Assembly, NYT School, and Sotheby’s.

L&D Best Practices for Employee Training
Written by
Amy Vidor
March 11, 2026
Create engaging training videos in 160+ languages.
Get started for FREE
In this article
Text Link
There’s plenty of advice on making employee training (including on this blog), but most of it skips the hard part:
building a strategy that makes training stick
.
This guide fixes that. We’ll focus on foundations: set up the infrastructure (even if you’ve already started), create feedback loops that keep training tied to real work, optimize for the business outcomes that matter, and scale deliberately as demand grows. Often the answer isn’t more content, tools, or headcount. It’s learning to deploy what you already have so training becomes a system that drives measurable impact.

📚 Key terms (click to expand)

Adoption:
Sustained behavior change over time, not just completion.

Capability building:
Long-term organizational ability to perform, adapt, and sustain outcomes.

Competency framework:
A defined set of skills, behaviors, and proficiency levels that describe “what good looks like” in a role.

Enablement:
Ongoing support that helps people perform in context, especially when work changes.

L&D (Learning & Development):
The function and operating model responsible for developing people at scale.

Learning in the flow of work:
Guidance and practice embedded where people work (tools, moments of need), not only in a course.

Readiness:
Confidence and correctness at launch (people know what to do and can do it).

Skills mapping:
Connecting skills and proficiency levels to roles, performance expectations, and career pathways.

Time to proficiency:
How long it takes someone to reach the expected performance level for a role.

Training:
Structured learning designed to build consistent role performance.

1. Start with a skills architecture
If training isn’t tied to a shared definition of skills, it’s hard to prove progress. You can ship great content and still struggle to answer the questions leaders care about: What capability are we building? Who needs it? What does “proficient” look like? How will we know performance improved?
A skills architecture gives you that foundation. It’s a practical system that defines the skills that matter (core, functional, and role-specific), sets 2–3 proficiency levels with observable behaviors, maps required skills to roles and levels, and specifies what counts as evidence (rubrics, QA checks, work samples, observations). It also needs governance: a named owner, a change process, and a review cadence.
Skills mapping should read like this:
‍
Skill → How you train it → How you practice → How you verify → What you measure.

Skills mapping example

Role:
Customer Support Specialist

Business driver:
Faster ramp, fewer escalations, higher quality

Diagnosis

Training:
Product + workflow walkthrough clips

Practice:
Troubleshooting scenarios

Evidence:
Scenario score + first-week ticket review

Metric:
First-contact resolution, rework rate

Tool fluency

Training:
Task-based “how-to” videos (tag, route, escalate)

Practice:
Guided sandbox tasks

Evidence:
Task checklist + supervisor sign-off

Metric:
Handle time, documentation accuracy

Escalation judgment

Training:
Escalation rules + examples

Practice:
“Escalate or resolve?” decision drills

Evidence:
Decision accuracy + QA sampling

Metric:
Escalation rate, time-to-resolution

Review cadence:
Quarterly (evergreen), immediate (policy/process changes)

Owner:
Support Enablement + QA (monthly signal review with team leads)

👉
Start here:
Pick one business-critical role and define 6–10 skills with 2–3 proficiency levels and one evidence method per skill.
2. Design intentional partnerships
Training stays relevant when you build reliable inputs from the teams closest to hiring, performance, and change. These partnerships aren’t about adding more approvers. They create signal loops so you can spot skill gaps early, adjust quickly, and keep learning
tied to business needs.
A partnership model includes a small set of core partners (HRBP or People Partner, a functional leader, and an enablement lead — plus Talent Acquisition when hiring is a constraint). Run a simple signal loop: a 30-minute monthly review focused on what’s changing in work and where performance is slipping. Use a lightweight intake so requests are comparable (business driver, audience, skill gap, success metric, constraints). Then do a quarterly reset to re-rank priorities based on business impact and capacity.
Use partners to surface specific signals:
Talent Acquisition:
Which skill gaps show up in hiring? What should we hire for vs. develop?
HRBPs / People Partners:
Where do performance conversations get stuck? What skills block progression?
Functional leaders:
What changed in the work? Where are errors, delays, or rework increasing?
Enablement leaders (Sales, CS, IT, Ops):
What do high performers do differently? What do new hires struggle with in the first 30–90 days?

Partnership cadence example

Monthly (30 minutes):
Signal review with HRBP/People Partner + functional lead + enablement lead

Quarterly (60 minutes):
Reset priorities with Talent Acquisition + functional leadership

Per request:
Use a one-page intake so every project stays tied to an outcome

One-page intake (copy/paste)

Business driver:
What needs to improve (quality, speed, customer outcomes, risk)

Audience:
Who needs to change behavior (role, level, region)

Skill gap:
What people can’t do yet (use skill language, not “needs training”)

Evidence:
How you’ll know it improved (manager observation, QA, system metrics)

Constraints:
Timeline, tools, compliance, localization

👉
Start here:
Set a 30-minute monthly signal review with one HRBP and one functional leader, using a one-page intake that captures business driver, skill gap, and success metric.
3. Set outcomes that matter
Training earns attention when it’s anchored to outcomes the
business already recognizes and reviews
. That means moving past “learning objectives” and defining performance outcomes instead: what people should do differently at work, and what should improve as a result.
Start with the business driver. Then set 2–3 outcomes you can track over time, using the same language leaders use to run the business (quality, speed, customer outcomes, risk, cost). Make the proof explicit: define what counts as evidence, capture the baseline before launch, and set a review rhythm so the program gets iterated as work changes.

Outcome mapping example

Business driver:
Improve customer experience while reducing rework

Audience:
New support hires (first 90 days)

Performance outcomes (2–3):
Increase first-contact resolution, reduce documentation errors, shorten time to proficiency

Evidence:
QA sampling + manager observation checklist + scenario score

Measures:
FCR %, documentation error rate, median time-to-proficiency

Review rhythm:
Baseline → 30 days → 90 days (iterate what isn’t moving)

👉
Start here:
Write one business-driver sentence, then choose two performance outcomes and one evidence method for each before building any content.
4. Design for skill transfer
Training only matters when it shows up in real work. Skill transfer is the bridge between “people learned something” and “
performance changed
.” The work environment is part of the design: peer support, manager coaching, and organizational reinforcement determine whether new behaviors stick after the session ends.
Design for transfer by building job practice into the workflow (scenarios and tasks that mirror real tickets and decisions), pairing it with clear feedback (rubrics, examples, coaching prompts), reinforcing it after launch (spaced follow-ups, reminders, refreshers), and validating it with a lightweight proficiency check tied to actual work.

Transfer example

Skill:
Escalation judgment

Job practice:
8 decision drills (“Escalate or resolve?”) using real edge cases

Feedback:
A simple rubric + a short “why” for each choice (what good looks like)

Evidence:
QA spot check on the first 10 tickets + manager observation checklist

Reinforcement:
Two-week follow-up with 3 new edge-case scenarios

Supporting content:
5-minute explainer with examples of correct vs. incorrect escalation

👉
Start here:
Take one high-impact skill and add one practice scenario plus a simple rubric or manager checklist that proves proficiency.
5. Deliver learning in the flow of work
Most training fails at the handoff: the moment someone needs to apply it. People don’t forget because they’re careless. They forget because work is busy, systems are complex, and support isn’t available at the point of need.
Learning in the flow of work closes that gap by embedding guidance where decisions happen. When support sits inside the workflow, it reduces guesswork, makes “the standard” easier to follow, and turns training into day-to-day performance support.
Design it around four pieces: identify the moments of need (exceptions, handoffs, first-time tasks), build small in-flow assets (checklists, decision aids, short clips, templates), place them inside the tools and workflows people already use, and iterate based on real breakdown points and usage signals.

In-flow support example

Process:
Handling a billing dispute

Moment of need:
A customer escalates and the agent needs to assess a policy exception

In-flow assets:
One-page decision tree, 60-second walkthrough clip, approved response template

Placement:
Linked inside the ticketing tool and pinned in the SOP

Evidence:
Manager spot check of 5 tickets per rep, per month

Measures:
Reopen rate, time-to-resolution, policy exception rate

👉
Start here:
Pick one error-prone workflow and publish a single in-flow asset (checklist, decision aid, or 60-second clip) inside the tool where the work happens.
6. Make managers your multiplier
Managers are the fastest path from “completed training” to “
changed behavior.
” They translate the standard into day-to-day expectations, create practice moments in real work, and reinforce what “good” looks like when things get messy. When managers coach to the same standard, training stops being an event and starts becoming performance.
Give managers a lightweight kit: define the 1–2 behaviors that signal success for the skill, provide three coaching prompts they can use in 1:1s or huddles, use a simple observation method (checklist or rubric) tied to real work, and identify the practice moments where managers can watch, coach, and confirm proficiency.

Manager toolkit example

Skill:
Escalation judgment

Standard:
Escalate only when criteria are met and clearly document the “why” in the ticket.

Practice moment:
Review 3 live tickets per rep each week for two weeks.

Coaching prompts:

“What signals led you to escalate (or not)?”

“Which criterion did this case meet? What would have changed your decision?”

“How would you summarize your decision in one sentence for the next team?”

Observation method:
Checklist covering correct criteria, complete documentation, and a clear next step.

Evidence:
QA spot check + completed manager checklist.

Measures:
Escalation rate, time-to-resolution, reopen rate.

👉 Start here:
Pick one high-impact skill and give managers a one-page kit (standard, 3 prompts, checklist) they can use in the next team meeting.
7. Treat content like a product
L&D can borrow a lot from product management. Product teams don’t ship once and move on. They assign ownership, manage versions, and release updates so customers trust what they’re using. Training should work the same way.
When content is managed like a product, it stays accurate through change, scales across teams, and improves over time. That’s an
operating model challenge
as much as a content challenge.
A product-style content model looks like this: one named owner per module, clear versioning (last updated + short change log), modular design so updates don’t trigger rebuilds, a predictable maintenance cadence plus an “urgent patch” path for policy changes, shared templates and standards for scripts/scenes/assessments/job aids, and a backlog driven by signals (QA findings, adoption issues, drop-off, stakeholder input). If you scale globally, bake in a localization workflow from the start: glossary, translation, and regional review.

Content operations model example

Content unit:
One topic, task, or decision (≤ 5 minutes)

Owner:
Named role (e.g., Enablement Lead) accountable for accuracy and updates

Single source of truth:
One library location with clear naming and tags

Versioning:
Version number + last-updated date + short change note

Refresh cadence:
Quarterly for evergreen content; immediate for compliance/process changes

Update triggers:
Policy changes, tool releases, recurring QA issues, or high drop-off

Templates:
Script, scene, assessment, and job-aid templates for consistency

Localization:
Approved glossary + translation workflow + regional review checkpoint

👉 Start here:
Pick one training “product,” assign a single owner, and add two basics: version + last-updated date, and a brief change log.
8. Prove impact with performance data
If you want training to function as a
business lever
, measure it like one. Completions and satisfaction scores tell you whether the experience landed. Performance data tells you whether capability improved.
Anchor each program to a clear business driver. Define the 2–3 outcomes that should move, using the same language leaders use to run the business (quality, cycle time, error rate, time to proficiency). Decide what on-the-job behavior will signal progress, capture the baseline before launch, and set a defined review point to decide whether to adjust, stop, or scale.
Training earns credibility when its results show up in the same dashboards as the work.

Measurement example

Program:
New discovery methodology training for Sales

Business driver:
Improve win rate and forecast quality

Performance metrics (2–3):
Discovery-to-next-step conversion, pipeline created per rep, win rate on qualified opportunities

Behavior signal:
Call review rubric on 2 calls per rep per month (talk track, qualification depth, next-step clarity)

Baseline:
Last quarter averages by segment (SMB/MM/ENT) before rollout

Data sources:
CRM stages + pipeline reports, call recordings, manager scorecards

Decision point:
If conversion doesn’t move, add targeted scenario practice for the weakest rubric dimension (for example: handling pricing pushback)

👉 Start here:
Pick one program and define two performance metrics plus one on-the-job behavior signal you can measure from baseline through rollout.
9. Use AI to scale personalization
Personalization is where L&D can move from “one program for everyone” to targeted support that actually changes performance. The goal isn’t novelty. It’s precision at scale: the right practice, in the right sequence, for the right role and proficiency level. That shift is already happening.
Teams expect AI
to drive value most through improved learner experience and personalization, with growing planned use in areas like personalized pathways, assessments, and skills mapping.
Keep personalization grounded in work. Tailor by role, proficiency level, and context. Use simple adaptive logic (“if this gap shows up, then this comes next”), and prioritize practice that matches real workflows: scenarios, drills, and checks that mirror the job. To keep it safe and consistent, lock personalization to approved sources and terminology, keep human review in the loop, and manage versions like any other content. Then improve the recommendations using real signals — assessment results, QA patterns, manager checklists, and usage.

Personalized training example

Program:
Global new-hire onboarding

Goal:
Faster time to proficiency with consistent standards

Core library:
Short AI video modules for tools, workflows, policies, and “what good looks like”

Personalization:

By role:
Sales vs Support vs Ops scenarios and workflows

By region:
Regional policy and terminology variations

By proficiency:
Foundational path → proficient path with harder scenarios

Signals to adapt:
Scenario scores, manager checklists, QA patterns

👉 Start here:
Pick one role and split one learning path into two proficiency levels (foundational and proficient), then use AI to generate role-specific practice questions and scenarios for each level.
10. Scale globally with AI video
AI video training isn’t a replacement for in-person training, live problem solving, or the kind of relationship-building that happens when teams learn together. Those moments still matter, especially for leadership, strategy, and complex change. What
has
changed is scale. AI video makes it practical to deliver consistent training across regions, keep it current as work evolves, and reach people in the flow of work, in the language and context they need. That direction aligns with
how leading organizations are rethinking development
: less “leave work to go learn,” more learning embedded into how work gets done.
To make it work in practice, you need a clear global baseline for “what good looks like,” a template system so modules stay consistent, a localization workflow that includes glossary + translation + regional review, and an update model with versioning and a fast path for policy or process changes. Put a named owner behind it, with a clear approval path, so accuracy doesn’t drift over time.

Scaling AI video with Synthesia example

Program:
Global onboarding for a customer-facing team

Core library:
A standardized set of AI videos (tools, workflows, policies, “what good looks like”)

Templates:
The same intro, structure, and call-to-action across every module

Localization:
Region-specific terminology and policy variants using an approved glossary + regional review

Updates:
Script edits and video regeneration when processes change, without reshoots

Versioning:
v1.3 + last-updated date + 3-line change log in the module description

Governance:
One global owner, with time-boxed regional approval for local policy differences

👉 Start here:
Use Synthesia’s
text-to-video tool
to turn one global onboarding script into a short AI video module.
Key Takeaways
The strongest employee training programs drive business impact by tying learning to skills, on-the-job performance, and progression — and then improving that system over time.
Build the infrastructure first. Stay close to change through tight partnerships. Design for transfer so new skills show up in real work. Measure impact with performance data. Scale deliberately: use AI to personalize practice and AI video to deliver consistent training across roles, regions, and languages.
If you want momentum fast, start narrow. Pick one role, one workflow, and one outcome you can measure. Ship a first version, learn from the signals, and expand from there.

Frequently asked questions
What are L&D best practices for employee training?
L&D best practices are repeatable methods for building workforce capability at scale. The strongest programs start with skills and performance requirements, align learning to measurable outcomes, deliver practice-based experiences, keep content current through governance, and measure impact beyond completion rates. In 2026, many teams are also using AI to improve personalization and speed up iteration, so learning stays relevant as work changes.
How do I design experiential, scenario-based training that changes behavior?
Design around real decisions people make on the job. Use scenarios that mirror your workflows, include realistic constraints, and require learners to choose an action, see consequences, and try again. Add quick feedback loops (manager debriefs, peer review, or coached practice) so learners connect training to performance expectations.
What's the best way to keep training content up to date as processes evolve?
Treat training as a living asset with clear ownership and a refresh cadence. Use modular content (short videos and reusable building blocks), maintain templates for consistency, and set triggers for updates (process changes, policy changes, product releases). Review engagement and drop-off points using analytics, then prioritize updates where they will change outcomes fastest.
Which metrics should I track to measure training impact beyond completion rates?
Start with 2–3 business-linked measures that should change after training: time-to-proficiency, error rates, quality scores, customer outcomes, cycle time, or compliance exceptions. Pair those with behavior signals (assessment performance, scenario decisions, manager observation) and learner confidence. Use a structured evaluation approach during design and after launch so measurement supports iteration and impact.
How can AI video help us scale and localize training for global teams?
AI video helps teams ship consistent training faster, update content without reshoots, and localize for global audiences with far less overhead. That matters in 2026 because AI use in L&D is already common, and teams are focusing on personalization and scalable delivery. Use AI video to standardize core messages, create role-based variations, and refresh modules as processes change.

How to choose the best screen recorder
People use screen recording for training, but also in other situations. And different video use cases require different features. Here are several use cases you may have and the features to watch out for when picking your screen recording software.
Features to look out for when creating software tutorials:
You want screen recording software that lets you edit quickly, annotate the footage, and guide viewers on the screen with cursor effects and highlights of essential areas.
✅ Quick editing tools.
✅ Live recording effects (cursors, content zoom, draw-on-screen).
Features to look out for when recording online classes or webinars:
You want a screen recorder with high-quality video and audio, live-streaming recording, and options to schedule and automate recordings.
✅ High-quality, stable live-streaming.
✅ Webinar management features that can host multiple event users.
Features to look out for when making instructional videos:
You want to enhance the
instructional video
’s clarity, flow, and overall presentation.
✅ Rich editing features (text overlays, annotations, captions, trimming, transitions).
✅ Control over what portion of the screen to record.
Features to look out for when recording video calls:
You want screen recording software that captures video and audio from the call simultaneously, regardless of the applications used for the call.
✅ High-quality, synchronized audio and video.
✅ Integration with popular video conferencing platforms (Zoom, Skype, Microsoft Teams).
Features to look out for when capturing live streaming videos:
You want to record videos without delays/buffering and to be able to view them later or edit the capture.
✅ Real-time recording capabilities.
✅ Different saving formats.
Features to look out for when creating
product demos
:
You want to record videos that show the product clearly and in detail, from multiple angles, demonstrating its features.
✅ Control recording specific application windows.

put a human face at the center of the message to guide, explain, and connect.
A visible speaker adds structure, context, and presence that screen recordings or slides alone often lack.
Synthesia offers a wide range of talking head video templates powered by

, making it easy to get started.

1)
Training video
For
training and educational videos
, a talking head works well because it mirrors the classroom dynamic. Learners are used to receiving instruction from a person, and a visible instructor can help structure the lesson, highlight key points, and make complex topics feel more approachable.
2)
Interactive quiz video
In
quizzes and interactive videos
, a talking head helps guide the learner through the experience, explain questions, and provide feedback in a way that feels more like a conversation than a test. Seeing a presenter introduces a sense of presence and pacing, which can make learners more comfortable and focused as they move through each step.
3)
Product demo video
In
product demos and tours
, a talking head can act as a guide who walks the viewer through features and workflows. This human layer helps frame what they are seeing on screen, provides context for why something matters, and creates a smoother narrative than screen recordings alone.
4)
Sales outreach video
In sales and outreach videos, a talking head makes the message feel more personal than text or slides. It allows the presenter to address the viewer directly, introduce an offer or idea, and communicate tone and intent clearly, which is especially important in first-touch or follow-up communication.
5)
Business presentation video
For
corporate updates and business presentations
, a talking head adds clarity and structure. A presenter can introduce topics, transition between sections, and emphasize key messages, helping the audience follow along as they would in a live meeting or all-hands presentation.
6)
Knowledge base video
In
knowledge base videos
, a talking head can provide quick orientation and explanation. A visible narrator helps set context, explain processes, and make otherwise static information feel more guided and easier to absorb.
7)
Recruitment video
‍
In recruitment and HR content, a talking head is useful for introducing the company, explaining roles or processes, and setting expectations. Seeing a person speak can help candidates and employees better understand who they are hearing from and what the organization is like, making the information feel more relatable and grounded.
8) Social media video
For social media videos, a talking head helps capture attention quickly and build a personal connection in short-form content. A presenter can deliver messages directly to the camera, making announcements, tips, or thought leadership feel more authentic and engaging in fast-scrolling feeds.
9. Educational video
In
educational videos
, a talking head supports explanation and continuity across lessons. Seeing the same instructor helps learners follow complex topics, maintain focus, and build familiarity throughout a course or learning program.
10. SOP video
For
standard operating procedure videos
, a talking head can introduce each step, explain why it matters, and guide viewers through the workflow. This human narration reduces ambiguity and makes procedural content easier to follow and remember.
11. Marketing video
In marketing videos, a talking head helps humanize the brand and clearly communicate value propositions. A presenter can frame benefits, tell short stories, and build trust in a way that feels more persuasive than slides or text alone.
12. Onboarding video
In
onboarding videos
, a talking head creates a welcoming first impression and sets expectations for new employees or customers. A visible host can guide viewers through what to expect and what to do next, making the experience feel more personal and reassuring.
13. Microlearning video
In
microlearning videos
, a talking head delivers short, focused explanations that feel direct and easy to digest. A presenter can introduce a single concept, provide quick context, and reinforce key takeaways in a highly efficient format.
14. Company culture video
In company culture videos, a talking head helps convey values, mission, and ways of working through real human presence. Seeing a spokesperson or leader speak makes cultural messages feel more authentic and emotionally engaging.
What is a talking-head video?
A talking head video is a type of video that features a person talking directly to the camera. The camera is usually positioned so that only the person's head and shoulders are visible.
Talking head videos are often used for educational or informational purposes, as they allow the viewer to hear the speaker's voice and see their expressions.
They can be used to deliver a lecture, give instructions, or provide commentary on current events.
They are also commonly used in marketing and advertising, as they can be very effective in delivering a message.
Why use a talking head in your videos
Using a talking head in your videos is the best way to:
✔️
Build a connection:
A face your audience identifies with can create a personal connection, build trust and credibility, and improve information retention.
✔️
Improve comprehension:
Facial expressions and body language reinforce the message and make a more impactful video.
✔️
Increase engagement:
A talking head keeps your audience engaged and interested in the video since people are likelier to pay attention when seeing a face.
Tips for filming talking head video content
The following tips will help you create talking heads videos of all types.
#1: Try using an AI avatar
One of the hardest parts about filming talking head videos is getting your production quality right. If you want to produce
instructional videos
at scale, consider using an
AI spokesperson
. There are hundreds of faces and voices to choose from.
#2: Make sure your audio is crystal clear
These days, even your iPhone camera can deliver great production value. But you'll still need to invest in an external microphone solution. A built-in microphone will pick up too much background noise, resulting in plenty of awkward pauses! If you're looking for a cheap solution, lapel mics usually do the trick. Else a high-quality boom mic is your best option.
#3: Lighting is the difference between amateur and expert
Professional studio lights can take any video clip from ugly to stunning. While you can also include natural lighting in your setup, make sure that you soften all shadows from your light sources using the principle of
3-point lighting.
#4: Use different angles to keep your audience's attention
All video types need to have a variety of video camera angles to be engaging and interesting to watch. When video editing, ensure you don't hold the same angle for an extended time. On the flip side, when your presenter is delivering key messages, it's best to keep the camera angle steady to avoid distraction.

Breaking through language barriers can open up exciting new opportunities for your videos.
For businesses,
AI video translation
means reaching new markets and connecting with diverse customers. Content creators can grow their audience. Educators can make lessons accessible worldwide.
The right video translation software saves time, enhances accuracy, and helps you reach viewers in their own language.

🌍 What's the best AI video translation tool?

Synthesia
: Best overall for business: highest-quality lip-sync, voice cloning, and enterprise-ready workflows.

AI Studios
: Best free and budget option for lip-synced dubbing (up to 3 minutes free, cheapest per-minute rates).

Perso AI
: Cheapest paid option for lip-synced dubbing, but you have to upgrade to download your video.

ElevenLabs
: Best for voiceover-only dubbing with ultra-realistic voice cloning.

Maestra
: Clunky interface and lip-sync is enterprise-only, but good value for large-volume translation projects.

Kapwing
: Good if you want video editing and basic dubbing in one tool.

Speechify
: Voiceover-only dubbing with limited control and inconsistent translation quality.

Murf
: Generous free voiceover minutes, but no lip-sync and voice cloning is enterprise-only.

Veed
: All-in-one editor, but no free plan and below-average dubbing quality.

Rask AI
: Expensive, and the lip-sync quality is very poor.

What are the different ways to translate a video?
When
translating a video
, you have two options:
Subtitles
: Translating spoken content into written text displayed on-screen. Adding subtitles to videos allow viewers to read the translation while hearing the original audio, which keeps the original voices and emotions intact.
Dubbing
: Translating and replacing the original audio with a new track in the target language. This can be standard
voiceover dubbing
, where the video stays the same, or
AI lip-sync dubbing
, where the video is altered so the speaker’s mouth movements match the translated speech.
How I test AI video translation software

🈯️ What makes a great AI video translator app?

Accuracy
– How accurate are the subtitles generated? How accurate is the dubbed speech? Does the translation sound natural to a native speaker?

Voice cloning
– Does the dubbed voice sound like the original person, or is it a robotic-sounding AI voice?

Lip-sync
– Does the video visually adjust to match the new dubbed voice?

Editing features
– AI translations aren’t always perfect. You need to be able to edit subtitles, scripts, and audio to fix mistakes.

Language support
– How many languages can the tool translate into?

Ease of use
– Is the interface intuitive and easy to learn?

Pricing
– Is the service good value for money?

‍1.‎ Synthesia
What I liked
The highest quality lip-sync of any AI dubbing tool on this list
The voice cloning works really well and sounds exactly like me
Wide range of languages supported (139+)
Offers an API and workflows that help you translate videos at scale
What I didn't like

What happened when I tried it
Synthesia offers
free AI dubbing with lip-sync
for videos up to 1 minute long. You can upload videos in .mp4, .mov, or .webm formats.
You can also use Synthesia to
translate a YouTube video
.
I found Synthesia’s AI dubbing tool super easy to use. I think the lip-sync quality is the best of any tool on this list.
The mouth movements look spot on and the timing works really well - the pacing, pauses and emphasis are close enough to the original that it still feels like my video, just in another language.
The translation sounds accurate to a native Spanish speaker’s ears.
Synthesia gives you the option of choosing “Adaptive" video length, which adjusts the video length for the natural speed that selected translation language is spoken at, which is super useful for some languages (e.g. German with its long compound nouns).
The platform also gives you a lot of flexibility after the initial dub is complete. After I’d watched the dubbed video, I opened the transcript editor and could see the full original script alongside the translated version, broken up into segments that matched the timing of the video.
I think this is super useful if you’re dubbing a video in a professional setting and terminology is touchy (e.g. product names, acronyms, bits of legal language). It lets you click into the translated text and correct the wording or tone.
Pricing
Synthesia lets you translate videos up to 1 minute long for free with full AI dubbing and lip-sync.
For longer videos, you'll need to sign up to the Starter plan for $29/month which gives you access to 10 minutes of AI dubbing with lip-sync at a rate of $2.90 per minute. Check out
our pricing
.
{lite-youtube videoid="l32HrQ-LwZI" style="background-image:url('https://img.youtube.com/vi/l32HrQ-LwZI/maxresdefault.jpg');" }
How does it compare to the other options?
Synthesia's AI dubbing offering is aimed at enterprise use cases who are looking for very high quality AI dubbing and functionality like secure editing or dubbing at large scale and/or via API. It's less suitable for individual creators on a budget.
Who should use it?
Synthesia's AI dubbing is suitable for anyone who needs AI video translation, but I think it makes the most sense for users who need a really high quality translation, which is typically anyone translating videos in a business context.

🎯 Why is Synthesia's AI dubbing the best choice for enterprise?

Built for serious training and comms, not just social clips

Optimized for long-form L&D, compliance, safety and product training, where accuracy, consistency and accessibility matter more than flashy one-offs.

One secure platform for creation + localization

Teams script, create, dub, approve, and publish in Synthesia — with templates, interactivity, SCORM, analytics and brand kit — instead of stitching together 3–4 separate tools.

Governance that matches enterprise risk profiles

SSO-protected video pages, org/workspace-level roles, brand kit enforcement, and pronunciation controls make it safe to roll out dubbing across large orgs with strict brand and compliance rules.

Editing controls that protect meaning

Secure translation and transcript editing, translation guidelines and glossaries help legal, compliance and SMEs fix wording while preserving intent and regulatory language.

Scales to whole catalogues, not just a handful of videos

API and Excel add-in support, templates, and bulk flows let you systematically dub libraries of training, onboarding and product content, with tracking instead of ad-hoc uploads.

Anchored in enterprise-grade support and workflows

Designed around procurement, admin, and reporting needs (credits, permissions, analytics, integrations), so dubbing is something IT and compliance can sign off on — not a shadow tool teams sneak in.

The most affordable rate for lip-synced AI dubbing (of acceptable quality) on this list

What I didn't like

What happened when I tried it
I really liked using AI Studios.
They let you do AI dubbing with lip-sync on videos up to 3 minutes long with a free account, which is the most generous of any tools on this list.
The translation is accurate, and in general the lip-sync quality is reasonable. I think the voice cloning works pretty well too - it sounds more or less like me.
AI Studios supports dubbing into 150 languages, so it's highly likely that they offer any language that you're after.
I played around a bit with the post-dubbing editing features and they were pretty solid too. You can refine the dubbed script to improve the timing, flow and accuracy which is great for avoiding additional generations and burning through all your credits.
The main issue I ran into with AI Studios was that the lip-sync drifted and there was some visible jittering in a few moments (you can spot it near the end of the video above). It’s the kind of thing I wouldn’t want in any video that really matters, especially in a professional setting.
However, if you're just using the free version for a quick translation of a video, then this might not matter much.
Pricing
AI Studios allows up to 3 minutes of AI dubbing a month on the Free plan. If you need more, you can buy the Personal plan for $29/month and get 120 minutes of dubbing allowance at a rate of $0.24/minute
How does it compare to the other options?
AI Studios offers AI dubbing with lip-sync of intermediate quality, but where it excels is its affordability.
It has the most generous free allowance for AI dubbing (with lip-sync) of all the tools in the list, and it also has the lowest cost per minute for additional AI dubbing minutes.
Who should use it?
I think AI Studios is a great option for those looking for quick AI video translation with lip-sync on a budget. The quality isn't to a super-professional standard, but if that doesn't matter for your use case, then I don't see why you use any other tool.
3. Perso AI
What I liked
Affordable lip-synced AI dubbing
Decent voice cloning
What I didn't like
You can't download your translated video on the Free plan
What happened when I tried it
Perso AI's lip-sync quality is pretty good, but it’s not at the level where I’d fully trust it for a high-stakes, polished business video. You can spot small timing issues and subtle mismatches, which are fine for quick demos or social content, but a bit distracting if you’re aiming for a very professional result.
The voice cloning is solid though. In my test, the cloned voice sounded close enough to my real voice that it didn’t feel like a generic AI narrator.
Perso AI also supports more than 32 languages, which covers most common business and content use cases.
One limitation to be aware of is the free plan. You can generate the dubbed video, but you can’t actually download it unless you upgrade, which makes the free tier more of a preview than something you can use end-to-end.
On the editing side, Perso AI does let you go back and tweak the translated script and timing, which is useful if the automatic translation isn’t quite right. You can correct wording, adjust pacing, and regenerate sections without starting from scratch.
Pricing
Perso AI's free plan lets you dub 1 minute of video, but it doesn't let you export your video. You can download your videos on the Creator plan though ($6.99/month)
However, the Creator plan gives you 15 mins of dubbing with lip-sync, at cost of $0.47/minute.
How does it compare to the other options?
I think Perso AI is another good option, but I feel like if you're looking for AI dubbing with lip-sync, you'll probably go with Synthesia or AI Studios as those options have superior dubbing quality, and they also both let you download your translated video on the free plan.
Who should use it?
If you're on a budget but you want to use AI dubbing with lip-sync.

What I liked

Only supports 29 languages
Learning curve is a bit steep
What happened when I tried it
ElevenLabs is best known for its
AI voice generation
, and their Dubbing Studio is focused purely on high-quality voiceover translation, without any lip-sync.
In my tests, the voice cloning did a great job of preserving my tone and emotion, so the translated audio still sounded like me rather than a generic AI voice.
That said, I did notice a few strange moments in the output.
In the example above, when I say “compruébalo” (“check it out”), the intonation sounds a bit off and not quite natural. It’s a small thing, but in a professional video it’s the kind of detail that would need fixing.
The good news is that ElevenLabs gives you very granular editing controls.
You can tweak timing, pronunciation, tone, and phrasing, which makes it possible to correct these issues, although I found that the interface is a bit more advanced and comes with a learning curve.
In terms of language coverage, ElevenLabs supports 29 languages, mainly focused on the major global markets.
Pricing
The platform gives you 5 mins of automatic watermarked voiceover dubbing for free.
You can get access to ElevenLab's Dubbing Studio on the $5/month creator plan. That gets you 3 minutes per month of voiceover-only dubbing at a rate of $1.67/min, with additional minutes available for $1.50/min.
How does it compare to the other options?
The main difference between ElevenLabs and the other options on this list is that ElevenLabs offers no lip-sync.
However, the voice cloning is, as you might expect, one of the best of the tools listed here.
Who should use it?
I think ElevenLab's dubbing studio makes sense for creators who don't need lip-sync and are happy with voiceover dubbing only.
5.‎‎ Maestra
What I liked
Accurate translation with natural sounding Spanish
Cloned voice sounded just like me
Decent language coverage (support for more than 125 languages)
What I didn't like
The platform is super confusing to use
No voice cloning on the free plan
Lip-sync only available on the $200/month business plan
Pricing structure only really works for large translation projects
What happened when I tried it
One thing that I liked about Maestra was the accuracy of the translation and how natural the Spanish sounded. The wording felt human and fluent, and in most cases it matched what I actually said.
I didn’t love that voice cloning isn’t available on the free plan, although once I had paid and got voice cloning working, it sounded pretty spot on.
It took me quite a while to work out how to generate my translated video with the cloned voice. The platform isn't very user-friendly and it was quite frustrating trying to work out how to do simple tasks.
I didn't get to try the lip-sync as it's only available on the $200/month Business plan, and I didn't want to pay that much.
Pricing
Standard voiceover dubbing without voice cloning costs $0.41 per minute on the Basic plan ($49 for 120 minutes). Voice cloning becomes available on the Premium plan at $0.99 per minute ($99 for 100 minutes), while lip-sync dubbing requires the Business plan and costs $1.00 per minute ($200 for 200 minutes).
How does it compare to the other options?
Like Murf and Speechify, the free plan is highly limited by the lack of voice cloning.
Maestra's dubbing with lip-sync is still quite affordable in $ per minute terms, although not as cheap as AI Studios or Perso AI's.
The pricing structure makes sense for someone who needs to translate a lot of minutes, but doesn't really work if you only want to translate a quick video.
Who should use it?
Someone on a budget who has a large translation project.
6.‎ Kapwing
What I liked
Affordable pricing
Good voice cloning
Lots of useful editing features
What I didn't like
Lip-sync quality isn't great
Annoying restriction on dubbing short videos (less than 10 seconds long)
Some quality issues with default export options
Slightly confusing interface
What happened when I tried it
Kapwing makes it easy to translate videos quickly with subtitles and basic dubbing, and overall it’s a pretty accessible tool.
The interface is a bit overwhelming at first though, mainly because there’s so much other video editing functionality packed into the product. It took me a moment to find the dubbing and translation features among everything else.
The translation itself was solid. Subtitles were accurate, and the voice cloning sounded surprisingly good for a general-purpose video editor. However, the default export quality wasn’t great, and I noticed some roughness in the final video.
The lip-sync quality itself doesn't look that great either. I don't think the timing and the movements look very convincing.
One small but annoying limitation was that my video had to be at least 10 seconds long to run the dubbing, so I had to artificially extend it just to test the feature. On the plus side, Kapwing gives you a lot of post-editing control, so you can fine-tune subtitles, timing, and audio once the translation is done.
Kapwing supports dubbing into more than 40 languages.
Pricing
On Kapwing’s Pro plan, which costs $24 per month, you get up to 50 minutes of standard dubbing, working out to $0.48 per minute. Lip-sync dubbing is priced as an add-on on the same plan, with up to 30 minutes available, which equates to roughly $0.80 per minute on top of the base dubbing cost. When you combine the two, full lip-synced dubbing comes out at approximately $1.28 per minute.
How does it compare to the other options?
I think there are better options on this list than Kapwing. If I want lip-sync I'd prefer to use Synthesia, AI Studios, or Perso. If I just want voiceover dubbing I'd probably prefer to go with ElevenLabs.
I think it's quite similar to Veed (which is further down the list) in that it's a video editing platform with some dubbing functionality added on, but it's not a very good standalone dubbing solution.
Who should use it?
Users who want a video translation solution that comes with extensive video editing features.
7.‎ ‎Speechify
What I liked
Supports dubbing into 60+ languages
What I didn't like
No lip-sync (or at least I couldn't find it anywhere)
No voice cloning on the free plan
The translation wasn't quite right and changed the meaning of what I said
The platform was a bit buggy and got stuck a few times
It seems overpriced for what you get
What happened when I tried it
Speechify seems to be a voiceover dubbing-only tool.
First I tried the Free plan (with no voice cloning). The first thing I noticed is that the translation wasn’t quite accurate. It came out as “Echa un vistazo y verás cómo funciona,” but what I actually said was “Check it out,” which should be closer to “Échale un vistazo.” That’s how most of the other tools translated it too.
It might seem like a small difference, but the added “verás cómo funciona” changes the meaning to “and you’ll see how it works.” In a high-stakes or client-facing translation, these kinds of unprompted additions can be risky and could cause real problems.
I bought the Studio Starter plan to test out the voice cloning. Speechify is a bit different in that you have to clone your voice separately and then select that cloned voice when you translate your video, which is a bit of a nuisance - pretty much every other tool on this list just clones your voice automatically.
When I did get the voice cloning working, it sounded pretty weird as you can see in the video above. I don't pronounce "todos" in "Hola a todos" correctly, and I pronounce "doblar" (to dub) in a strange way that sounds like I'm a pirate.
Pricing
Speechify gives you 3 minutes and 20 seconds of voiceover dubbing on their Free plan. Beyond that you'll need their Studio Starter plan which costs $19/month and gives you 40 minutes of voiceover dubbing at a rate of $0.48/minute (and access to voice cloning).
Their documentation mentions that lip-sync is available, but I can't find it anywhere on their platform or on their pricing page.
How does it compare to the other options?
The Speechify platform looks and feels very similar to Perso AI's platform, but aside from that there aren't many similarities.
Since I couldn't find any details about any lip-sync functionality, it feels like Speechify is closer to Murf or ElevenLabs in that it only appears to offer voiceover dubbing.
It's kind of similar to Murf in that it doesn't offer voice cloning on the free plan too.
Who should use it?
I'm not really sure. I'd probably prefer to use ElevenLabs instead of Speechify.
8.‎ Murf
What I liked
100 minutes of voiceover dubbing on the free plan
What I didn't like
You can't download your translated video on the Free plan
No lip-sync available, voiceover dubbing only
Limited language options
Voice cloning only available on the Enterprise plan
What happened when I tried it
I was disappointed with Murf's dubbing solution.
Firstly, it's voiceover dubbing only, although you could argue that's fair enough since Murf is an AI voice-focused company.
While testing, I saw that the available language variations are super limited. For example, for Spanish they only offer Spanish (European) and Spanish (Mexico), and that's it.
While I was trying to download my translated video, I found that I couldn't export it as an MP4 (or any other format) without signing up for a paid plan. I understand these platforms have to make money but I found that a super annoying way to offer a free plan.
Lastly, I found that voice cloning functionality is only offered on the enterprise plan. It's understandable if the platform is largely geared at enterprise, but it really does make the tool less useful for the individual creator. I was instead stuck with one of the stock AI voices that you can hear on my video above. I think you'll agree it doesn't sound that great.
The one saving grace of Murf is that their Free plan allowance of 100 minutes of voiceover dubbing (without voice cloning) is still quite generous.
Murf supports dubbing into 40+ languages.
Pricing
Murf offers 100 minutes of voiceover dubbing to users on the Free plan. If you want additional minutes (and if you want to be able to export your videos) you'll need to pay a cost $0.5/minute in a pay as you go structure. Voice cloning is only available to enterprise users.
How does it compare to the other options?
Murf is similar to ElevenLabs in that it's primarily an AI voice generation platform that is offering a dubbing tool. As a result, there's no lip-sync functionality and it's entirely focused on voiceover dubbing.
The difference between Murf and ElevenLabs is that Murf really doesn't seem geared towards creators (whereas ElevenLabs absolutely is). The fact that Murf's voice cloning is only available to Enterprise plans is a big issue for me.
Who should use it?
If you need free voiceover dubbing minutes and don't care about voice cloning.
9.‎ ‎Veed
What I liked
Accurate translation
Veed has a nice interface with lots of other editing tools that might be useful
Dubbing into 125+ languages
What I didn't like
No freemium dubbing option
No freemium subtitles option
Lip-sync feels a bit off
Voice cloning didn't really work
What happened when I tried it
Although I was trying to test the freemium version of all of these tools, Veed doesn't offer any AI video translation functionality on their free plan, so I was forced to pay up just to even try it.
Veed has a nice interface and is easy to use. It's a potential advantage in that you can translate and then edit your video (e.g. add animations or transitions) all in one platform, but I personally didn't need any of that functionality.
There's an option to upload your own transcript too.
I particularly liked how the dubbed audio pronounced "Synthesia" in the way a natural Spanish speaker would. I selected the 'Match Video Voice' option but I don't think that the cloned voice sounds like me speaking Spanish.
Looking at the video again, I think the lip-sync is a bit off. If the tool was free I'd let that slide, but given that they made me pay I think that's not good enough.
Pricing
To access subtitle and AI dubbing video translation in Veed you'll need the Pro plan, which costs $55/month. The plan gives you 20 minutes of dubbing per month so that works out at a cost of $2.75/minute.
How does it compare to the other options?
I don't really see any benefits of using Veed's AI video translation tools. There's no free option, and the output isn't as good as some of the free options on this list.
Who should use it?
I don't really recommend Veed for AI video translation, but maybe it makes sense to use Veed if you want to do a bunch of editing to your video as well.
10.‎ ‎Rask AI
What I liked
Voice cloning quality wasn't bad
What I didn't like
You can't download your translated video on the Free plan
Very high price for voiceover dubbing ($2.40/minute)
Lip-sync quality is absolutely terrible
What happened when I tried it
Rask AI ended up being my least favourite tool on this list. The voice cloning quality itself wasn’t bad, and in isolation the generated voice sounded fairly natural.
On paper, it also looks strong with support for 135 languages, which is one of the widest language ranges I tested.
In practice though, the experience was frustrating.
You can’t download your translated video on the free plan. On top of that, the pricing for voiceover dubbing only is very high at around $2.40 per minute, which is similar to the cost of full dubbing with lip-sync on other platforms.
Rask's lip-sync is where things really fall apart. To even access it, you need the Creator Pro plan, which is extremely pricey. And from the previews I tested, the lip-sync quality was genuinely awful, with obvious mismatches and unnatural mouth movements. It was bad enough that I didn’t even bother paying just to export the result. I didn’t want to waste money on something I already knew I wouldn’t use.
Pricing
Rask AI's Creator plan offers 25 minutes of voiceover dubbing for $60/month (or $2.40). That cost per minute goes down a bit if you go for the $150/month Creator Pro plan (to $1.5/minute) which also gives you access to lip-sync.
How does it compare to the other options?
Badly. The cost of voiceover dubbing is equivalent to the cost of full AI dubbing with lip-sync on the other platforms in this list, yet Rask AI's lip-sync functionality appears to be almost broken.
Who should use it?
I don't recommend it for anybody.
