The 17 Best Employee Training Software & Platforms (2026)
Written by
Kevin Alster
December 18, 2025
Create engaging training videos in 160+ languages.
Get started for FREE
Text Link
This guide breaks down the best employee training software for
creating courses
in 2026, grouped by function, and grounded in real-world employee training use cases.
All tools were reviewed using the same evaluation approach, with a focus on practicality, scalability, and how they perform in day-to-day L&D work.

The best employee training software

🗂️ Learning Management Systems (LMS)

Moodle

TalentLMS

🧭 Course platforms & Learning Experience Platforms (LXP)

Kajabi

LearnWorlds

📚 Pre-made course providers & content libraries

LinkedIn Learning

Coursera

📈 Learning analytics & assessment tools

ClassMarker

Watershed

🛠️ Course authoring tools

Articulate Rise 360

Articulate Storyline 360

Adobe Captivate

Compozer

🎥 Video-based training tools

Synthesia

Vyond

✨ Microlearning & visual tools

Genially

Canva

🖥️ PowerPoint-based authoring

iSpring Suite

Creating effective training
today isn’t just about
authoring a course
, it’s about choosing the right mix of tools to build, deliver, assess, measure, and scale learning across an organization.
I’ve worked as an Instructional Designer for over seven years, building everything from onboarding and compliance programs to product education, certification pathways, and global learning initiatives.
In that time, I’ve tested dozens of training platforms across corporate, academic, and commercial environments.

🧪 How I evaluate employee training software

To keep the comparisons fair and practical, I evaluated each tool using the same set of criteria, focusing on how well it supports real-world L&D workflows rather than edge-case features.

📋 Evaluation criteria

Ease of setup and overall usability

Course creation or content delivery capabilities

Assessment and feedback options

Reporting and analytics

Integrations with LMSs and other platforms

Scalability for teams and organizations

AI-assisted features, where applicable

🧩 Standard test use case

To evaluate each platform consistently, I used a single, real-world use case: building a short training course on writing effective professional emails. This topic was chosen because it reflects a common workplace training need and requires a mix of content creation, structure, assessments, and learner engagement.

Each tool was tested on how efficiently it could support creating, delivering, or enhancing this course—whether through authoring, hosting, video creation, assessments, or analytics.

Learning Management Systems (LMS)
Tools that host, deliver, and track training programs.
Moodle

🎯 Best for

Academic institutions and universities

Large corporate L&D teams

Organizations needing full control over data and infrastructure

Complex assessments and conditional learning paths

Compliance-driven or regulated environments

🚫 Not ideal for

Small teams without technical or admin support

Fast, no-setup LMS deployments

Teams prioritizing modern UX out of the box

Rapid content authoring workflows

✅ Pros

Extremely flexible and customizable

Powerful and robust assessment engine

Open-source with full control and ownership

Supports SCORM, xAPI, and cmi5

Large plugin ecosystem

⚠️ Cons

Steeper learning curve

Requires technical resources for setup and maintenance

Less modern UI without theming

Slower content creation workflows

💰 Pricing
Moodle itself is free to use when self-hosted, but in practice you still need to budget for hosting, maintenance, security, and ongoing administration.
For teams that want a managed setup, MoodleCloud and enterprise hosting options are available, with pricing varying depending on scale and support requirements.
My experience with Moodle
Moodle feels like a platform that prioritizes control and flexibility over speed. I think it’s designed less for quick launches and more for organizations that need to run structured learning programs with a lot of rules and complexity.
It works especially well when you’re dealing with advanced assessments, conditional learning paths, or strict compliance requirements, where having full ownership over the system really matters
That flexibility does come with trade-offs. Moodle typically requires more upfront setup and ongoing maintenance than modern SaaS LMSs, and without additional theming, the interface can feel dated.
Content creation is also slower, since Moodle is built primarily for delivery and management rather than rapid authoring.
For teams with technical or administrative support, those compromises are usually worth it.
For smaller teams, Moodle can feel heavy, but as a long-term learning platform, it’s very capable.
TalentLMS

🎯 Best for

Small to mid-sized L&D teams

Fast rollout of internal training or onboarding

Compliance-focused corporate training

Teams without a dedicated LMS administrator

AI-assisted course creation to speed up delivery

🚫 Not ideal for

Highly complex or multi-layered learning designs

Advanced interactivity, simulations, or branching

Teams needing deep customization or branding on lower tiers

✅ Pros

Very fast to implement

AI-assisted course creation

Strong compliance and completion tracking

Intuitive and easy-to-use interface

Practical integrations (SSO, HR tools, Zapier)

⚠️ Cons

Limited advanced authoring capabilities

Less flexibility for complex learning designs

AI-generated content requires review

Advanced customization locked behind higher tiers

💰 Pricing
TalentLMS pricing generally starts around $69/month USD for entry-level plans, with higher tiers unlocking additional features, additional users, and more customization options. Enterprise pricing is available for larger organizations with more complex requirements.
My experience with TalentLMS
TalentLMS feels very much optimized for speed and simplicity.
I think it’s the kind of LMS you choose when the goal is to get training live quickly without dealing with technical setup or ongoing administration.
It works especially well for
onboarding
, internal training, and compliance programs where ease of use and reliability matter more than deep customization.
The
AI-assisted course creation
is one of the more practical features. Being able to generate outlines, lessons, and quizzes from prompts can noticeably reduce development time, as long as the content is reviewed and refined with instructional goals in mind.
Where TalentLMS shows its limits is in more complex learning design.
Advanced interactivity
, branching scenarios, or simulations aren’t really its strength.
Overall, it’s a clean, efficient platform that prioritizes fast implementation and smooth delivery over flexibility and depth.
Course platforms & Learning Experience Platforms (LXP)
Tools that combine course creation, delivery, and learner experience into a single platform.
Kajabi

🎯 Best for

Course creators, coaches, and consultants

Small training businesses selling paid programs

Memberships and cohort-based courses

Teams that want learning, marketing, and payments in one platform

Monetized education rather than internal corporate training

🚫 Not ideal for

Complex corporate L&D workflows

Standards-based learning environments

Advanced assessments or learner analytics

Large-scale internal training programs

✅ Pros

True all-in-one platform

Easy to use and quick to set up

Built-in marketing, payments, and automation

Clean learner experience

Reduces need for multiple tools

⚠️ Cons

Not LMS-grade reporting or tracking

No SCORM, xAPI, or cmi5 support

Limited assessment capabilities

Higher cost as scale increases

💰 Pricing
Kajabi plans typically start around $149/month USD, with higher tiers unlocking increased automation limits, larger contact volumes, and more advanced features.
Costs are worth evaluating carefully for organizations planning to scale large learner audiences or run long-term programs.
My experience with Kajabi
Kajabi feels much more like a business platform than a traditional LMS.
I found that it works best when the primary goal is selling and delivering learning, rather than managing formal training programs.
Everything from course delivery to websites, payments, email marketing, and automations lives in one place, which removes a lot of operational friction if you’re running paid courses or memberships.
That all-in-one approach is also where the trade-offs show up. Kajabi isn’t built for standards-based tracking or complex L&D scenarios, and the lack of
SCORM
or xAPI support makes it a poor fit for organizations that rely on structured reporting or external authoring tools. Reporting and assessments are fairly lightweight compared to enterprise LMSs.
Overall, Kajabi shines as a delivery and monetization platform, but it’s best viewed as an experience and business layer rather than a full LMS replacement.
LearnWorlds

🎯 Best for

Course creators focused on polished, engaging learning

L&D teams delivering customer or partner training

Video-centric learning programs

Teams prioritizing branding and presentation

Organizations selling or distributing online courses

🚫 Not ideal for

Highly regulated or compliance-heavy environments

Standards-based learning ecosystems

Complex corporate LMS workflows

Advanced learning path logic and reporting

✅ Pros

Strong interactive video capabilities

Easy and fast course creation

Built-in engagement and learner analytics

Modern interface with strong branding control

End-to-end course delivery in one platform

⚠️ Cons

Limited SCORM and xAPI support

Less flexible than a full LMS

Lighter reporting and learning logic

Costs increase as scale and features grow

💰 Pricing
LearnWorlds pricing generally starts in the $29–$99/month USD range, with higher tiers unlocking advanced analytics, branding options, and enterprise features.
Exact pricing depends on the level of customization and scale required.
My experience with LearnWorlds
LearnWorlds feels very clearly optimized around learner experience, especially for
video-based courses
.
In my experience, it’s best suited for teams that care deeply about how learning looks and feels, rather than those trying to replicate a traditional LMS.
The interactive video capabilities stand out, with the ability to embed questions, buttons, and overlays directly into videos, which can make courses feel far more engaging than standard video lessons.
That focus on experience does come with some limitations. LearnWorlds isn’t designed for standards-heavy or highly complex L&D setups, and limited SCORM and xAPI support can be a blocker if you rely on external authoring tools or need advanced tracking.
Reporting and learning logic are also lighter than what you’d expect from an enterprise LMS.
Overall, LearnWorlds works best as a polished delivery platform for external or commercial learning, rather than a system built for deep corporate training infrastructure.
Pre-made course providers & content libraries
Tools that provide ready-to-use learning content rather than custom course creation.
LinkedIn Learning

🎯 Best for

Organizations offering self-directed professional development

Continuous learning and upskilling initiatives

Soft skills and technical skill development

Teams that don’t want to build courses in-house

Individuals focused on career growth

🚫 Not ideal for

Internal training tied to company-specific workflows

Custom course creation or tailored messaging

Advanced assessments or detailed learner control

Organizations needing LMS-grade tracking

✅ Pros

Massive professional content library

High production quality

Strong professional and brand credibility

Personalized recommendations

Certificates tied to LinkedIn profiles

⚠️ Cons

No custom content creation

Limited assessment and reporting control

Not tailored to internal training workflows

No SCORM or xAPI export

💰 Pricing
LinkedIn Learning is typically offered through individual subscriptions starting around $39.99/month USD. Enterprise pricing is available via LinkedIn Learning for Business, with costs varying based on organization size and licensing model.
My experience with LinkedIn Learning
LinkedIn Learning feels best positioned as a content library rather than a training system.
I have found that it’s most useful when the goal is to give learners immediate access to high-quality professional development without investing time in course creation.
The breadth of topics and overall production quality stand out, especially for soft skills, leadership, and technical upskilling.
Where the platform shows its limits is customization. Because all content is pre-built, there’s no way to tailor courses to
internal tools
, processes, or messaging, and assessment and reporting are relatively lightweight.
It also works better as a supplemental resource than a primary LMS.
Overall, LinkedIn Learning is a strong option for continuous, self-directed learning, but it’s not designed to replace a full training infrastructure.
Coursera

🎯 Best for

Workforce upskilling and reskilling initiatives

Career-aligned, credentialed learning

Organizations valuing academic and industry recognition

Long-term development pathways

Individuals pursuing formal certifications

🚫 Not ideal for

Custom internal training programs

Company-specific workflows or tools

Just-in-time or microlearning needs

Standards-based LMS integrations

✅ Pros

Highly credible credentials

Strong academic and industry partnerships

Career-aligned, structured learning paths

Clear assessments and progression

Recognized certificates

⚠️ Cons

No content customization

Less flexible pacing

Not designed for internal training delivery

No SCORM or xAPI export

💰 Pricing
Coursera pricing varies depending on the course or certification, with individual programs priced separately.
Coursera for Business offers enterprise pricing based on the number of learners and level of access, which typically needs to be evaluated on a case-by-case basis.
My experience with Coursera
Coursera feels firmly positioned around formal, credentialed learning rather than internal training delivery.
In my experience, it works best when the goal is to offer learners access to recognized certifications or academically backed programs that support long-term career development.
The structure of the courses, along with graded assessments and defined progression, makes it well suited for reskilling and upskilling initiatives where credibility really matters.
That same structure can be limiting in other contexts. Coursera isn’t designed for customization, so there’s no way to tailor content to internal tools, workflows, or messaging.
Course pacing is also less flexible, which makes it harder to use for short, just-in-time learning needs.
Overall, Coursera works well as a formal learning and credentialing platform, but it’s better viewed as a complement to internal training systems rather than a replacement for them.
Learning analytics & assessment tools
Tools designed to test knowledge, support certifications, track learning data across platforms, and help measure training impact beyond completion.
ClassMarker

🎯 Best for

Compliance checks and certification exams

Post-training knowledge validation

Teams needing fast, secure assessments

Organizations already using another LMS

Lightweight assessment-only use cases

🚫 Not ideal for

End-to-end learning delivery

Course authoring or content hosting

Highly customized learner experiences

Complex learning journeys

✅ Pros

Fast and easy to use

Strong security and access controls

Clear and automatic reporting

Supports question banks and randomization

Well suited for compliance and certification

⚠️ Cons

Assessment-only tool

Limited customization

Not a full learning platform

Needs to be paired with other tools for delivery

💰 Pricing
ClassMarker pricing typically starts around $39/month USD, with plans scaling based on the number of tests, users, and security features required.
Higher tiers unlock additional administrative controls and customization options.
My experience with ClassMarker
ClassMarker feels purpose-built for assessment and nothing else. I think it works best when you need a fast, reliable way to test knowledge without the overhead of a full LMS.
Creating quizzes and exams is quick, results are automatically graded, and reporting is clear enough to immediately understand how learners performed.
The security features stand out for compliance and certification use cases, with options like passwords, time limits, and controlled access adding confidence when assessments matter.
At the same time, its limitations are very clear. There’s no course delivery, no broader learning journey, and only limited customization of the learner experience.
Overall, ClassMarker works well as a lightweight assessment layer alongside another platform, but it isn’t meant to manage learning end to end.
Watershed

🎯 Best for

Enterprise L&D teams

Organizations with mature learning ecosystems

Measuring learning impact and ROI

Teams using multiple LMSs and learning tools

L&D teams with analytics or data support

🚫 Not ideal for

Small or early-stage L&D teams

Teams without technical or analytics expertise

Content creation or course delivery

Simple, single-platform learning setups

Enterprise-grade analytics

Strong xAPI support

Excellent reporting flexibility

Aggregates learning data across systems

Moves beyond completion-based metrics

⚠️ Cons

Not beginner-friendly

Requires technical expertise

Not suitable for small L&D teams

No content creation or delivery

💰 Pricing
Watershed uses an enterprise pricing model, with costs varying based on data volume, integrations, and reporting requirements.
Pricing is provided through custom quotes and is typically aligned with large or complex learning ecosystems.
My experience with Watershed
Watershed feels like a platform built for organizations that are serious about measuring learning impact, not just tracking completions.
In my experience, it works best when learning data is already spread across multiple systems and there’s a real need to bring everything into one place.
By acting as both a Learning Record Store and analytics layer, it helps connect LMS data, xAPI activity, and learning experiences that would otherwise live in silos.
That depth comes with complexity. Watershed isn’t something you can plug in casually, and teams without technical or analytics support may find the setup challenging, especially when integrating multiple data sources.
It also isn’t designed to deliver or
create learning
, so it only makes sense as part of a broader ecosystem.
Overall, Watershed is a strong fit for enterprise teams that need advanced reporting and are ready to invest in learning analytics, but it’s more than smaller or simpler environments usually need.
Course authoring tools
Tools used to design and build custom eLearning content, from rapid microlearning to highly interactive, scenario-based courses.
Articulate Rise 360

🎯 Best for

Rapid course creation for L&D teams

Onboarding, compliance, and internal communications

Microlearning and modular training content

Teams prioritizing speed and consistency

Instructional designers working closely with subject-matter experts

🚫 Not ideal for

Highly customized course design

Advanced branching or simulations

Deeply interactive learning experiences

Teams needing full design control in a single tool

✅ Pros

Fully responsive by default

Modern, clean course design

Very fast and easy to use

Well suited for microlearning

Low-friction authoring experience

⚠️ Cons

Limited advanced interactivity

Less design control than advanced authoring tools

Courses can feel uniform at scale

💰 Pricing
Articulate Rise is included as part of the Articulate 360 subscription, which typically costs around $1,099/year USD per user.
The subscription also includes Storyline 360 along with collaboration features and a shared asset library.
My experience with Articulate Rise
Articulate Rise feels purpose-built for speed. I've found that it’s one of the easiest ways to turn structured content into a polished, professional-looking course without needing design or technical expertise.
The block-based editor makes it simple to organize lessons, and the fact that everything is fully responsive by default removes a lot of complexity, especially for teams delivering content across devices.
That simplicity is also where Rise draws its boundaries. Design and interaction options are intentionally constrained, which helps with consistency but limits flexibility.
For more complex branching, simulations, or custom interactions, Rise on its own isn’t enough, and it often needs to be paired with a more advanced tool like Storyline.
Overall, Rise works best as a rapid authoring tool for standard training formats, where clarity, speed, and consistency matter more than deep interactivity.
Articulate Storyline 360

🎯 Best for

Instructional designers needing full control over interactivity

Complex, scenario-based and simulation training

Custom eLearning for corporate L&D teams

Agencies and freelance instructional designers

Projects requiring standards-based LMS delivery

🚫 Not ideal for

Rapid or last-minute course creation

Teams without dedicated instructional design resources

Browser-based or Mac-only workflows

Simple linear training content

✅ Pros

Powerful customization and control

Great for complex interactions and branching

Robust publishing options

Well suited for advanced assessments and simulations

⚠️ Cons

Not designed for rapid authoring

Steep learning curve

Desktop-based and Windows-only

Longer development cycles

💰 Pricing
Articulate Storyline is included as part of the Articulate 360 subscription, which typically costs around $1,099/year USD per user.
The subscription also includes Rise, Review 360, and additional collaboration and asset tools.
My experience with Articulate Storyline
Articulate Storyline feels like the tool you reach for when learning design requirements get serious.
I think it shines when you need precise control over how learners move through content, especially for branching scenarios, simulations, and highly interactive courses.
The ability to work with triggers, variables, layers, and states makes it possible to build experiences that go far beyond linear slides.
That level of control comes at a cost. Storyline isn’t fast to learn or to build in, and development cycles are noticeably longer compared to rapid authoring tools like Rise.
Since it’s desktop-based and Windows-only, it can also be limiting for some teams.
Overall, Storyline is best suited for teams with dedicated instructional design expertise who need depth and flexibility, rather than speed or simplicity.

Responsive technical training content

L&D teams needing advanced interaction control

💰 Pricing
Adobe Captivate is typically available via subscription at approximately $33.99/month USD, with enterprise licensing options also available for larger organizations.
My experience with Adobe Captivate
Adobe Captivate feels very purpose-built for technical training.
In my experience, it’s strongest when you’re creating step-by-step software simulations or system walkthroughs where precision really matters.
The simulation tools make it easier to capture and structure detailed workflows, and the support for responsive design helps courses adapt across devices without rebuilding everything from scratch.
That power comes with complexity. Captivate’s interface feels more technical than newer authoring tools, and without a large library of visual templates or assets, more design effort is often required.
It’s not a tool I’d reach for when speed is the priority, but for experienced instructional designers working on technical or process-heavy training, Captivate offers a lot of control and depth.
Compozer

🎯 Best for

Subject-matter experts creating training content

Compozer pricing typically starts around $108/month USD for smaller teams, with higher-tier and enterprise plans available for larger organizations or teams requiring advanced collaboration features.
My experience with Compozer
Compozer feels designed to get subject-matter experts directly involved in course creation.
I think it works best in environments where training content needs to be updated frequently and shared ownership matters more than polished, custom design.
The browser-based editor is approachable, and the built-in collaboration features make it easy for multiple contributors to work on the same content without heavy coordination.
That simplicity does come with trade-offs. Compozer isn’t built for complex learning design, and advanced interactions or custom visuals are limited.
Courses can start to feel templated if the structure isn’t carefully planned.
Overall, it’s a solid fit for organizations that want to decentralize content creation and move faster, but it’s not the right tool for highly bespoke or interaction-heavy eLearning.

My experience with Synthesia

video creation

In my experience, it’s most valuable when video needs to be produced quickly, consistently, and at scale, especially across different teams or languages.
Turning scripts into presenter-style videos

AI avatar

That efficiency does come with boundaries. Synthesia isn’t meant to replace full video editing tools, and options for cinematic control are more limited.
Overall, it works best as a scalable video layer in an L&D stack, where speed, consistency, and multilingual delivery matter.

My experience with Vyond
Vyond feels purpose-built for storytelling.
In my opinion, Vyond works best when training relies on scenarios and narrative rather than direct instruction.
The animated characters and scenes make it easier to represent real-world situations, especially in HR, compliance, or behavioral training where using live actors isn’t practical or appropriate.
That storytelling power comes with a time trade-off. Building animated videos in Vyond generally takes longer than script-to-video tools, and it’s not designed for realistic video or rapid content iteration.
I also found that the browser-based editor can also feel slower on heavier projects.
Overall, Vyond is a strong fit for teams that value narrative and engagement over speed, and that want animated scenarios as a core part of their training approach.

Genially feels designed to make learning more interactive without adding technical overhead.
I think Genially works best for short, engagement-driven experiences like
microlearning

That focus on interaction also defines its limits.
Genially isn’t built for complex instructional logic or deep branching, and while SCORM export is available, tracking options are lighter than in dedicated authoring tools.
Performance can also be impacted if projects rely heavily on animations or media.
Overall, Genially works best as a complementary tool that adds interactivity and visual interest to a broader learning ecosystem, rather than as a standalone course authoring solution.

My experience with Canva

produce presentations

The templates and drag-and-drop editor make it easy to create content that looks polished and consistent.
At the same time, Canva isn’t meant to deliver learning on its own. There’s no learner tracking, assessments, or standards-based output, so it needs to be paired with an LMS or authoring tool.
Overall, Canva works best as a supporting layer in an L&D stack, helping teams move faster and maintain visual quality rather than managing training end to end.
PowerPoint-based authoring

iSpring Suite

🎯 Best for

PowerPoint-based eLearning workflows

Subject-matter experts comfortable working in PowerPoint

iSpring Suite is typically licensed annually, with pricing starting around $770/year USD per author. Volume discounts and enterprise licensing options are available for larger teams.
My experience with iSpring Suite
iSpring Suite feels designed to meet teams where they already are.
It’s one of the easiest ways to
turn existing PowerPoint decks into trackable eLearning
without introducing a completely new authoring environment.
Because everything happens inside PowerPoint, most users can start building courses almost immediately, which makes it especially useful when timelines are tight.
That familiarity also sets the boundaries. Courses tend to follow a linear, slide-based structure, and while quizzes, narration, and screen recordings are easy to add, more advanced interactivity or creative layouts are limited compared to tools like Storyline or Captivate.
Overall, iSpring works best as a practical, low-friction solution for scaling eLearning quickly using existing content, rather than as a tool for highly custom learning design.
How to choose the right employee training software
The most effective employee training software stacks are built with intention, not stitched together over time. Choosing the right tools isn’t about finding one platform that does everything. It starts with understanding your training objectives and selecting software that works well together.
Some companies need to train large, distributed teams quickly. Others require more tailored programs, detailed assessments, or deeper reporting. The best decisions come from clarity around who the employees are, what skills or behaviors need to change, and how training success will be measured.
Internal capacity matters just as much as features. Software that looks powerful on paper can slow teams down if it requires technical skills or resources you don’t have. In many cases, a simpler employee training tool that’s easy to use will deliver better results than a complex system that never gets fully adopted. Evaluating tools based on real training scenarios rather than feature lists helps expose these trade-offs early.
How employee training software can work together
In reality, most teams don’t rely on a single employee training platform. Training software ecosystems are usually made up of multiple tools, each serving a specific role.
Content is often created in authoring tools and then delivered through an LMS or employee training platform. Video tools, microlearning platforms, and design software support these programs by improving engagement and retention. Assessment and analytics tools typically sit alongside this setup, helping teams validate learning outcomes and measure impact across systems.
When chosen deliberately, these tools complement one another and give organizations the flexibility to design employee training programs that are both engaging and measurable.
When training software is used independently
Not every organization needs a fully connected training ecosystem. In some cases, employee training software is used independently to solve a specific need.
A company might use a course library to quickly upskill employees without creating custom content. Design or presentation tools may support internal communications or just-in-time training on their own. Other platforms can function as standalone solutions for customer education, partner training, or paid courses.
Independence doesn’t mean inefficiency. It means alignment. The value of employee training software comes from how well it fits its role, not from how many features it includes.
Final thoughts
There’s no single “best” employee training software, only the best setup for your organization. Strong training teams choose tools based on learner needs, internal resources, and long-term goals rather than chasing feature checklists.
When selected with intention, modern employee training software can work together to create learning experiences that scale, engage employees, and support real performance improvement.

Frequently asked questions
What features should I prioritize when evaluating employee training software for my organization?
When evaluating employee training software, prioritize features that directly support your learning objectives and make training accessible for your entire team. Look for intuitive content creation tools that let you build courses quickly without technical expertise, robust tracking and reporting capabilities to measure learning impact, and strong integration options with your existing HR and productivity tools. Mobile accessibility ensures employees can learn anywhere, while multilingual support becomes crucial for global teams.
Beyond the basics, focus on features that drive engagement and retention. Interactive elements like quizzes and scenarios keep learners actively involved, while personalization options help deliver relevant content to different roles and skill levels. Consider whether you need video creation capabilities for more engaging content, microlearning support for busy employees, and collaborative features that let subject matter experts contribute directly to course development. The right combination depends on your team size, industry requirements, and whether you're focused on compliance training, skills development, or ongoing professional growth.
How does Synthesia fit alongside an LMS and other training tools in an L&D tech stack?
Synthesia serves as the video creation layer in your L&D tech stack, working seamlessly with your LMS and other training platforms rather than replacing them. While your LMS handles course delivery, tracking, and learner management, Synthesia enables you to create professional training videos quickly from scripts, eliminating the need for cameras, actors, or production teams. These videos can be exported and uploaded directly to your LMS, embedded in courses created with authoring tools like Articulate or Captivate, or integrated into microlearning platforms.
This complementary approach lets each tool do what it does best. Your LMS remains the central hub for learning delivery and analytics, while Synthesia accelerates content creation and helps you scale video production across teams and languages. For example, you might use Synthesia to create onboarding videos that live in your LMS, product training updates that integrate with your knowledge base, or multilingual safety videos that support your compliance program. By adding Synthesia to your existing tech stack, you enhance your training content without disrupting established workflows or requiring teams to learn entirely new systems.
How can I create and update multilingual training videos at scale without filming or editing skills?
Creating multilingual training videos at scale becomes manageable when you use AI-powered video creation tools that work directly from scripts. Start by writing your training content in your primary language, focusing on clear, concise messaging that translates well across cultures. Modern AI video platforms can then generate presenter-led videos with AI avatars speaking your script naturally in over 140 languages, eliminating the need for multiple filming sessions, voice actors, or complex editing workflows. This approach lets subject matter experts and L&D teams create professional videos in minutes rather than weeks.
The real advantage comes in maintaining and updating content across languages. When policies change or products update, you simply edit the master script and regenerate videos in all required languages simultaneously. This ensures consistency across global teams while dramatically reducing the time and cost traditionally associated with multilingual video production. Teams can maintain version control, ensure compliance across regions, and deliver culturally appropriate training without managing multiple production workflows or coordinating with translation agencies for each update.
What are best practices for rolling out employee training software company-wide to drive adoption?
Successful company-wide rollouts start with securing executive sponsorship and identifying champions across different departments who can advocate for the new training platform. Begin with a pilot program in one department or team, gathering feedback and refining your approach before expanding. Create a clear communication plan that explains not just how to use the software, but why it matters for each employee's development and success. Make the first training experiences positive by launching with high-value, immediately applicable content that demonstrates the platform's benefits.
Drive ongoing adoption by removing friction at every step. Ensure single sign-on integration so employees don't need another password, embed training links directly in existing workflows, and start with short, focused modules that respect busy schedules. Regular communication about new content, recognition for completion milestones, and visible support from leadership all reinforce the importance of training. Track adoption metrics closely in the first 90 days, addressing technical issues quickly and celebrating early wins to build momentum across the organization.
How can I measure the impact of employee training beyond completion rates and quizzes?
Measuring true training impact requires connecting learning activities to business outcomes and behavioral changes. Start by establishing baseline metrics before training begins, such as productivity levels, error rates, customer satisfaction scores, or time-to-competency for specific tasks. Then track these same metrics after training to identify improvements. Use manager observations and 360-degree feedback to assess whether employees are applying new skills on the job, and conduct follow-up surveys at 30, 60, and 90 days to measure knowledge retention and confidence levels.
Advanced measurement approaches include analyzing performance data from business systems to correlate training completion with improved results. For sales training, track changes in conversion rates or deal sizes. For customer service training, monitor resolution times and satisfaction scores. For compliance training, measure incident rates and audit results. Combine quantitative data with qualitative insights from focus groups and interviews to understand not just what changed, but why. This comprehensive approach to measurement helps justify training investments and continuously improve program effectiveness based on real business impact.

What are employee training videos?
Employee training videos are used to help people learn how to perform tasks, use tools, or respond to situations in their work. They are most effective when they are designed around what someone needs to do after watching, not just what information they need to see.
‍
What are common use cases for employee training videos?
Common use cases include:
Software and systems training
Procedural and SOP training
Compliance and safety training
Customer service and sales training
Leadership and management training

What types of training videos should I create?
Training videos are often described as types such as how-to videos, screen recordings, or scenario-based videos.
In practice, these are elements that are combined depending on the outcome. A single video might include a walkthrough, a short explanation, and a scenario that shows how the task plays out.
How do I create effective employee training videos?
Start by defining the outcome:
After watching this video, employees will be able to…
From there, structure the video around that outcome and include the elements needed to support it. Templates can help you apply a consistent structure and update training as work changes.
‍
Why are many training videos not effective?
Many training videos are created and shared but only watched once. They often focus on explaining information instead of helping people apply it in their work.
Effective training videos are designed for use in real situations and can be revisited when needed.
How does AI help create training videos?
AI video platforms make it easier to produce, update, and scale training content.
This reduces production constraints and allows teams to focus on designing training that supports performance, rather than just creating content.
What is the best format for a training video?
There isn’t a single best format.
The right structure depends on the outcome. Most effective training videos combine different elements, such as walkthroughs, explanations, and scenarios, to support how the learner will use the information.

Voice replication and
AI text-to-speech
technology are rapidly changing how we interact with digital devices. While these advancements offer significant benefits, such as enhanced user experiences and accessibility, they also raise substantial ethical considerations. This article discusses the ethics of cloning, covering privacy, misuse risks, and essential safety measures.
The promise of cloning technology
Voice cloning
technology creates highly realistic synthetic voices from a small sample of someone's speech. This technology is especially useful in areas like customer service, where it offers personalized communication without needing constant human effort. According to a 2021 study by
Juniper Research
, the number of voice-assisted devices is expected to exceed 8 billion by 2023, doubling from just 4 billion in 2020. This rapid growth underscores the increasing reliance on voice technology across various sectors.
Ethical concerns and privacy issues
Cloning raises many ethical and privacy issues that we must address to protect individual rights and maintain trust in communication technology. As the use of synthesized voices becomes more widespread, distinguishing between authentic and artificial voices becomes more difficult, posing intricate challenges for ethical governance and usage.
1. Consent and ownership
One of the primary ethical concerns with cloning is the need for clear consent and ownership. Ethical use of this technology requires explicit permission from the individuals whose voices are being cloned. Ensuring that individuals are fully aware of how their voice will be used is crucial for maintaining personal autonomy and dignity.
2. Potential for misuse
The potential misuse of voice replication technology can range from creating misleading or fraudulent audio clips to impersonating others without their consent. Such scenarios can lead to significant trust issues and legal implications, particularly in the realms of misinformation and identity theft.
A detailed report by
Pindrop
noted a 350% increase in voice fraud incidents from 2013 to 2017. In one noted case, fraudsters used synthetic voice technology to impersonate a CEO’s voice and successfully requested a fraudulent wire transfer of $243,000.
3. Privacy preservation
Protecting the privacy of individuals whose voices are cloned is paramount. This requires implementing secure data handling practices to prevent unauthorized access to and use of voice samples, which could breach privacy.
Regulatory framework and compliance
Managing the ethics of cloning needs strong regulatory frameworks. Effective rules should ensure that the collection, use, and storage of voice data are transparent and open for review. Regulators must enforce stringent consent protocols that are clear, informed, and revocable at any time by the data subject. Additionally, implementing comprehensive data protection measures is crucial to safeguard personal information against unauthorized access and misuse.
Meeting existing legal standards is pivotal for responsibly deploying cloning technologies. In Europe, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) provides a solid foundation for the protection of personal data, emphasizing the rights of individuals to control their personal information and setting strict guidelines on consent. Since the implementation of GDPR in Europe, there have been significant advancements in how voice data is managed. For instance, under GDPR, users have the 'right to be forgotten,' which has led to stronger controls and the ability to erase personal data upon request—a crucial protection in the realm of voice replication.
Similarly, in the United States, the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) sets standards for the protection of personal health information, ensuring that data privacy is maintained in healthcare-related cloning applications.
These regulations should be seamlessly integrated into the lifecycle of
voice cloning
technologies, from initial development through to deployment and beyond. Companies and developers should engage with legal experts and policymakers to ensure full compliance, adapting their operations as legal frameworks evolve. This adherence not only mitigates legal risks but also builds public trust in voice technologies, paving the way for their ethical and sustainable use.
Implementing ethical practices in cloning
As cloning technology advances, organizations must embed ethical considerations deeply within their operational practices. This involves not only adhering to legal standards but also actively cultivating a culture of ethical awareness. By prioritizing ethical practices, companies can navigate the complexities of this innovative technology responsibly, ensuring that its application benefits society while minimizing potential harm. The following points elaborate on key areas such as transparency, security, ethical AI frameworks, and the importance of regular audits in maintaining the integrity and trustworthiness of cloning applications.
1. Transparency
Companies need to be clear about how they use cloning technology. This includes informing users about the use of synthetic voices and the purposes for which they are employed.
2. Security measures
Adopting stringent security measures to safeguard voice data is crucial. This means encrypting voice samples and using access controls so only authorized people can use the data
3. Ethical AI frameworks
Developing and following ethical AI frameworks can guide the responsible use of voice replication technologies. These frameworks should address concerns such as fairness, accountability, and the societal impact of the technology.
4. Regular audits
Conducting regular audits can help ensure compliance with ethical standards and regulations. These audits should assess both the technology itself and its broader impacts on society.
An ethical approach to cloning in practice
Synthesia is an AI video generation company that offers cloning in addition to AI avatar technology to allow users to create studio-quality videos in minutes. As a leader in the AI video generation space, Synthesia adheres to a strict ethical framework known as the
3Cs—Consent, Control, and Collaboration
—to guide its use of synthetic media technologies. This framework ensures that all AI-generated content respects the rights of individuals and maintains high ethical standards.
Consent
: Synthesia ensures real human actors consent to the use of their likenesses for creating AI avatars, thus respecting personal and image rights.
Control
: The company implements rigorous content moderation policies and uses technology to prevent the misuse of its platform, ensuring that the content generated remains appropriate and secure.
Collaboration
: Engaging with regulatory bodies and participating in industry-wide initiatives, Synthesia actively promotes the development of robust AI policies and ethical standards.
Ensuring ethical integrity in voice technology
Voice replication technology holds immense potential, but its ethical implementation is crucial for building trust and ensuring compliance with legal standards. By addressing the ethical challenges head-on, developers and users of this technology can mitigate risks and maximize its benefits, ensuring it serves the greater good. As we continue to integrate voice technology into our lives, staying vigilant about these ethical considerations will remain a top priority.

Today, we’re thrilled to introduce an experimental feature that will take the AI avatar experience to the next level:
Selfie Avatars
. With just a few images of yourself, you can create a custom avatar that opens up new possibilities for expression and communication.
This feature marks an exciting milestone for Synthesia as we continue to innovate and shape the next generation of AI avatars coming later this year.
Let’s dive into what this feature is all about, how it works, and the safeguards we’ve built into the system to ensure it’s safe and inclusive for everyone.
A sneak peek into the future of avatars
The Selfie Avatar feature is part of our vision to give users more control and creative freedom over their digital identities. After uploading a small set of selfies, you’ll be able to prompt for your avatar in any outfit or physical environment. Then, you can use the avatar to generate short-form video clips by
recording an avatar voiceover
.
This experimental release is your chance to be part of this journey and provide valuable feedback that will help shape the evolution of AI avatars. But this is just the beginning; in the near future, our new EXPRESS-2 model will allow users to control even more of their avatars’ performance, including body language.
Being transparent about the technical limitations
As with any experimental technology, there are some limitations. While we’ve worked hard to make Selfie Avatars as accurate and realistic as possible, you might encounter occasional issues during the generation process.
For example:
The avatar may not always capture your physical likeness perfectly.
There may be instances where details like facial expressions or proportions differ slightly from your expectations.
We want to be upfront about these limitations because your feedback during this phase is essential. Your insights will help us refine the technology and ensure that the final version of this feature exceeds expectations.
Building a safe and responsible platform
At Synthesia, we take the responsible development of AI seriously. With the launch of this experimental feature, we’ve invested heavily in red teaming efforts to identify and mitigate potential risks, including working with
Risky Business Solutions
—a team of experts in trust and safety-related issues.
Here’s how we’re ensuring a safe and positive experience for everyone:
Prevention of harmful content
: We’ve implemented robust safeguards and new policies to prevent the generation of hate symbols, nudity, sexually explicit content, and other harmful materials. This ensures that our platform remains inclusive and respectful.
Impersonation controls
: We’ve designed the system to minimize the risk of impersonation, protecting individuals from unauthorized use of their likeness. For example, we’re the only platform to require a biometric consent flow during the Selfie Avatar creation process, which minimizes the risk of non-consensual deepfakes.
AI bias mitigations
: Image generators amplify bias in gender and race, despite efforts to improve the quality of the data sets and models producing these results. We’ve taken steps to fine-tune the third party image generator we’re using during the avatar creation process but we know that our system isn’t perfect.
Responsible AI principles
: Our development process is guided by a commitment to responsible AI practices, ensuring that our technology benefits society while minimizing potential misuse.
Join us on this journey
The Selfie Avatars feature represents a glimpse into the future of digital identity and customization. While it’s still in an experimental phase, we’re excited to invite you to try it out, share your thoughts, and help us shape what’s next.
We’re eager to hear your feedback, whether it’s about the quality of the avatar, your overall experience, or how we can improve the feature. Together, we can create a platform that’s not only innovative, but also safe, ethical, and empowering for everyone.

Written by
Elly Henriksen
June 25, 2024

Text Link
To find our what makes B2B explainer videos stand out from the crowd, we analyzed 9 popular video examples.
All these B2B explainer videos had a few things in common:
Varied, engaging visuals, often switching between actors, visualizations, and footage.
Fast-paced timing between shots, with no time wasted on long explanations.
A memorable storyline and CTA made each video uniquely interesting.
Want to learn how to do the same? Check out these examples for inspiration.👇
1. Product explainer for machinery
Machinery is complicated. But
this
short B2B explainer video makes the TC-2000 Series Machine less intimidating, especially in how it gets the message across in only 68 seconds!
The presenter's casual look brings a fresh modern feel and makes the complex topic of machinery approachable. Meanwhile, the visuals give an easy feel for what the machinery does. We see moving cogwheels, software interface snapshots, and on-screen text that perfectly syncs with the narration.
This video is a great example for anyone looking to showcase tech without getting lost in the jargon or scaring the target audience away.
2. Meet WatsonX from IBM
IBM's "Meet WatsonX" offers a sleek visual representation of complex ideas in the world of AI and data platforms. It could easily be at the forefront of a video marketing campaign.
In under two minutes, it creates a visual spectacle of overlapping circles in cool shades of blue. While the visuals capture your attention, they don't distract from the message because all those symbols beautifully represent the interconnected data and AI processes.
3. CEO announcement of an AI-driven CRM
This video example
is an elegant blend of vision and innovation, packed swiftly in only one minute and a half. Zyva's CEO Jordan Ellis, dressed sharply in dark grey and pink, sets a professional yet approachable tone. The visuals — a mix of pink and grey — mirror the company's forward-thinking pivot.
Throughout the video, Ellis shifts from dominating the screen to sharing space with timelines and text. Visuals cleverly reflect Zyva's journey from traditional CRM to leading-edge AI solutions.
This isn't just an announcement. It's the story of a transformation.
4. What is Hootsuite?
This video's storyline starts with a relatable analogy of businesses feeling left out of the "social party." But then, it quickly pivots to show how Hootsuite is the perfect plus-one for businesses who need social media management.
The video's friendly and conversational tone is spot-on. It demystifies social media strategy without dumbing it down. The visuals are straightforward and supportive, making complex features like scheduling, integration, and analytics seem like no-brainers.
5. Introducing travel insurance bundles as card perks
Within a 2-minute runtime,
SureSecure
positions its insurance offerings as a game changer for card companies. This neat, polished B2B video explainer addresses partners directly. It highlights the win-win of integrating travel insurance into card tiers.
Visuals and narration work hand-in-hand to clarify insurance jargon, making ideas easy to understand. It brilliantly segments the benefits across Standard, Gold, and Platinum cardholders. Doing so clarifies the value proposition and subtly encourages cardholders to aspire to higher tiers.
6. Why Klaviyo
Any business that wants to communicate its value proposition can learn from how Klaviyo is doing it. They invite you to seek deeper, more authentic customer connections without sacrificing growth.
Klaviyo's explainer starts from a strong premise: consumers crave human connections, not faceless interactions.
Using a series of live-action videos of people, the video introduces the Klaviyo platform as a unified solution that goes beyond email and SMS. The straightforward explanations, dynamic visuals, and compelling narration make complex concepts accessible. As for the overall message of empowerment and control over customer relationships and data, it hits home.
7. Monday Sales CRM
Monday's Sales CRM video demonstrates how to highlight user-friendly features and customization capabilities in a digestible format while building on your marketing funnel.
In a brisk 1 minute and 13 seconds, it distills the essence of what makes their CRM not just useful but desirable for sales teams.
The magic of this video lies in its clear, concise delivery. It goes straight for the benefits. They show the platform's intuitive design and how even the most complex sales tasks can become simple.
8. Ahrefs motion graphics explainer video
With no narration and only background music, this motion graphics animated explainer video is a masterclass in simplicity and clarity. The crisp, clean 2D animations guide viewers through the journey of a user's search experience. Removing the barrier of technical jargon, this engaging video speaks to both novices and those more experienced in the field.
Notice how the intuitive visuals and succinct text overlays cleverly illustrate Ahref's customer issues and how they can help them.
If you're looking for animated explainers with strong visual storytelling, this example might very well inspire your next B2B explainer video.
9. Slack Teams Do Amazing Things
Fans of animation videos and dynamic content will love this example. In just over a minute, you'll be reminded of how effective animated explainer videos can be.
Told entirely through charming animations, the video brilliantly ends with the USP: "
All kinds of people of all kinds of teams use Slack to do amazing things.
"
The expressive animations perfectly capture the essence of teamwork and productivity that Slack enables. Even more, these cute characters and their interactions illustrate how Slack streamlines communication and project management.
Like all good animated videos, this one is universally understandable. It's fun and relatable. And it paints the picture of Slack as a platform that brings teams together to achieve amazing things.
5 Speedy tips for creating an awesome explainer video
Whether hiring an agency or making your
marketing videos
in-house, these tips will help keep your video project on track.
Remember, a great B2B explainer video should always be working to get the "yes" from your customer. Packed with some of the best explainer videos, your marketing strategy can help you get:
More qualified leads from your website
A shorter lead time on new prospects
A marketing budget that's spent more efficiently
Here are 6 must-know tips for creating a great B2B explainer video.
Tip 1. Keep it under two minutes
An explainer video should be short, sweet, and to the point, ideally no longer than 90 seconds. You want to get your message across without boring your target audience or overwhelming them with too much information.
Anyone can cut a first 5-minute script draft down to 90 seconds, but the hard part is to do it and
still
get your point across. So, spend time on your explainer video script and imagine how the visuals and narration could work together to explain more in less time.
Tip 2. Use simple language
It's easy to forget that not everyone knows what you know
When writing your
explainer video script
, use simple language that everyone can understand. Avoid industry jargon or technical terms your audience might not be familiar with, and try to make the explainer video accessible to as many people as possible.
Audience research can help you understand what jargon and language your new customers use. This market research style is part of the wildly successful
customer-led growth framework
that thousands of marketers swear by.
Tip 3. Try an AI video generator
You might think it's impossible to bypass the filming stage of making a video, but thanks to technology, it is!
The
text-to-video
tool Synthesia can create realistic human avatars using AI and offers templates you can customize with your own live-action footage. It can even create voiceovers in 130+ languages and 400+ voices.
Tip 4. Tell a story
Stories are a powerful way to communicate information and can help people remember your video long after watching it. Creating a good story is easier said than done. Even Disney famously recycles scenes that tell a good story.
One way to create a story is to begin with the pain point or problem, agitate that problem, and position your product as the ultimate solution. This is called the PAS formula and has been used by marketers since the first newspaper ads.
Additionally, use industry
statistics
to illustrate the size of the problem. The numbers your explainer video offers lend it authority and make the viewers feel like they're not the only ones with those specific pain points.
Tip 5. Add your spin to stock footage
Most companies use stock footage and pre-made animated video elements to quickly and efficiently create great explainer videos. Some businesses even use stock graphics to create whiteboard explainer videos without ever picking up a camera.
But there's a problem with plain 'ol stock footage: It looks generic.
So, pay attention to the style of stock you choose and make sure it's aligned with your brand colors and the rest of the video.
6. Include a Call-to-Action (CTA) from the start
Many people quickly add a call to action at the end of their explainer video as an afterthought. If you want to create an effective video, you should do the opposite.
Start by thinking about what action you want your user to take after watching your explainer video. Then, work backward to figure out how best to convince them to take that next step.

A compelling story has the power to transform the world—or at least your business metrics.
Take this for example:
In 2009, a relatively unknown startup called Dropbox teamed up with explainer video pioneers Common Craft to create a 2-minute and 16-second masterpiece. The cost? $50,000. The impact? Staggering. The video, showcased on Dropbox’s homepage, racked up over 25 million views, drove more than 10 million signups, and generated upwards of $48 million in revenue 🤯.
While Dropbox’s success story remains legendary, the landscape of explainer videos has evolved significantly since then.
Today, whether you have a modest budget or big bucks to spend, you can choose from a range of professional explainer video companies or dive into
explainer video software
to create one yourself.
To help you navigate this dynamic market, we’ve rounded up the top 20 explainer video production companies of 2026. Let’s dive in!
How to choose an explainer video company
An explainer video is a short-form video made for marketing or sales purposes that highlights a company's product, service, or business idea compellingly and efficiently. So, plenty of video production companies can create such explainers, from AI-driven platforms to traditional animation studios.
When selecting an explainer video company, consider the following key factors to ensure your final video aligns with your vision and goals.
Portfolio & creativity
Look at the company's portfolio and see if you can picture your project there. Do their style and quality match what you're envisioning for your target audience?
Each brand and message is unique, so a one-size-fits-all creative approach rarely captures the audience's attention in explainer videos. Your chosen explainer video company should tailor its services to meet your needs and creatively convey your message.
Experience & expertise
An explainer video company that has worked on topics relevant to your industry or has a proven track record with similar clients can bring valuable insights and understanding to your project. These industry-specific insights will be useful, once again, for capturing the audience's attention with messages that resonate.
Look for a company with a well-structured
video production process
that aligns with your timeline, ensuring your project is completed efficiently and on schedule.
Cost and value
While
cost
is always a consideration, focus more on the value offered than just the price. For example, choosing an explainer video company that is responsive and open to collaboration will make the creative process smoother and more enjoyable for you. And that often means a better output.
It's also a good idea to find a company or solution that offers a streamlined process with additional services, such as marketing and distribution support, which can further fast-track your project.
Check if they're on trend with technology
Look on their blog and social media to see if the company values constantly learning and innovating in video production. The more innovative ideas an explainer video company embraces, the more it has an edge in creating engaging and relevant videos on a tighter budget.
Companies that utilize AI and productivity tools are adept at innovative ideas and can often offer you more bang for your buck. Most of their time is spent refining your video to suit your target audience and marketing funnel rather than doing the more mundane parts of
video creation
(such as resizing videos).

how to create an explainer video

What makes a good explainer video?
Be Unique—Stand Out from the Crowd
Your explainer video should be a reflection of your brand’s personality, not a carbon copy of what’s already out there. Find a fresh angle, use distinctive visuals, and make sure your message feels original.
Inject Humor to Boost Engagement
A little comedy can go a long way in making your video more shareable. A well-placed joke or lighthearted moment keeps viewers entertained while ensuring they remember your message.
Keep It Clear and Concise
The whole point of an explainer video is to simplify complex ideas, not overcomplicate them. Stick to the essentials and avoid unnecessary fluff to make your content easy to digest.
Know Your Audience
Think about who you're trying to reach and tailor your video style to their preferences. A playful, animated approach might work for a younger crowd, while a sleek, professional tone may be better suited for B2B audiences.
How to Make an Explainer Video
Before diving into video creation, take a moment to define your objectives. What do you want viewers to learn or do after watching? Once that’s clear, follow these key steps:
1) Craft a Strong Script
Every great explainer video starts with a solid script. A common framework includes:
Introducing a relatable problem
Envisioning a world where the problem is solved (“Imagine if…”)
Presenting your product or service as the perfect solution
2) Find the Right Voice Over Talent
A compelling voice over adds professionalism and keeps viewers engaged. While DIY recording is an option, hiring a professional often delivers better results. Platforms like
Fiverr
offer budget-friendly choices, while
VoiceBunny
provides higher-end options.
3) Select the Best Explainer Video Software
There are plenty of user-friendly tools designed for making explainer videos, many of which offer free trials. The right choice mostly depends on which type of explainer video you want to make...
What are the main types of explainer videos?
Live action
{lite-youtube videoid="wwm8TAKjN04" style="background-image:url('https://img.youtube.com/vi/wwm8TAKjN04/maxresdefault.jpg');" }
A
live-action explainer video
uses real people, settings, and props to demonstrate a product, service, or concept. This style builds trust and creates a personal connection with the audience, making it ideal for showcasing tangible products, company culture, or human-centered stories. It often involves professional filming, editing, and scripting for a polished look.
AI Avatar
{lite-youtube videoid="JkENp3eiPXA" style="background-image:url('https://img.youtube.com/vi/JkENp3eiPXA/maxresdefault.jpg');" }

{lite-youtube videoid="MlLw7KdEyA8" style="background-image:url('https://img.youtube.com/vi/MlLw7KdEyA8/maxresdefault.jpg');" }
A
2D animated explainer video
uses flat, two-dimensional graphics to convey a story or explain a concept. It’s characterized by its simplicity and versatility, making it ideal for engaging audiences and breaking down complex ideas in a visually appealing and easy-to-understand way.
3D animated
{lite-youtube videoid="U-Sv_pv6nkg" style="background-image:url('https://img.youtube.com/vi/U-Sv_pv6nkg/maxresdefault.jpg');" }
A
3D animated explainer video
uses three-dimensional visuals to create realistic or stylized representations of objects, characters, or environments. This style adds depth and detail, making it ideal for showcasing products, demonstrating complex processes, or creating immersive storytelling experiences. It’s especially effective for industries like technology, engineering, and architecture.
Whiteboard explainer
{lite-youtube videoid="7X3EcggN-84" style="background-image:url('https://img.youtube.com/vi/7X3EcggN-84/maxresdefault.jpg');" }
A
whiteboard explainer video
is a type of animation where illustrations and text are drawn on a whiteboard or white background, often accompanied by narration. It mimics the effect of someone teaching by drawing, making it highly engaging and effective for explaining complex concepts in a simple, visual way.
Stop-motion animated
{lite-youtube videoid="64hM5XuCVq4" style="background-image:url('https://img.youtube.com/vi/64hM5XuCVq4/maxresdefault.jpg');" }
A
stop-motion animated explainer video
is created by capturing a series of individual photos of physical objects or scenes, moving them slightly between each shot. When played in sequence, these images create the illusion of motion. This technique gives the video a unique, handcrafted feel, often used to convey creativity, charm, or authenticity.
Kinetic typography
{lite-youtube videoid="ZfomZ6EeWGs" style="background-image:url('https://img.youtube.com/vi/ZfomZ6EeWGs/maxresdefault.jpg');" }
A
kinetic typography explainer video
focuses on animated text to convey a message or tell a story. The text moves, transforms, and interacts dynamically with the screen, often synchronized with music or narration. This style is highly effective for emphasizing key points and creating an energetic, attention-grabbing presentation.
Screencast
{lite-youtube videoid="ASxoHquGoXc" style="background-image:url('https://img.youtube.com/vi/ASxoHquGoXc/maxresdefault.jpg');" }
A
screencast explainer video
is a recording of a computer or device screen, often paired with voiceover narration, to demonstrate how software, websites, or digital tools work. It’s an effective and straightforward way to guide viewers through processes or features step-by-step.
